records.label: exp14-risor-range-container
records.summary: The description is concise, direct, and retains the non-obvious behaviors exercised by the tests without unnecessary scaffolding.
records.description:
Make a range usable wherever the language accepts a sequence container. `len(r)` reports how many values the range produces, `r[i]` returns the value at position `i`, `r[i:j]` produces the values from position `i` up to position `j`, `v in r` reports whether `v` is one of the values the range produces, and `sorted(r)` returns those values in ascending order. A byte or a float equal to a value the range produces is one of them. Slicing a range yields a range. Assigning to a position of a range is not supported.

Every one of these except `sorted` is computed rather than produced: a range spanning 10^15 values answers all of them without producing its values. When a range produces more values than an integer can count, `len(r)` reports the largest representable integer, while indexing and membership stay defined over every value the range produces.

records.label: exp8-rhai-try-finally
records.summary: The description is direct and compact while retaining the semantics the hidden tests exercise.
records.description:
Add a `finally` block to Rhai's `try` statement.

A `try` statement may end with `finally { ... }`, with or without a `catch` clause before it. The `finally` block runs once after the `try` block is finished with, whether it completed normally, or raised an error that the `catch` clause handled, or is being left by `return`, `throw`, `break` or `continue`. An empty `finally` block still runs, and runs at the same points as any other.

The `finally` block also runs when the engine stops the script for exceeding its limit on operations, even though no `catch` clause handles that. It makes no difference where the limit was reached: a limit reached inside a call, including a call to `eval`, is still such a stop. Exceeding that limit does not stop the `finally` block from running its own statements: the block runs with its own allowance of operations, counted afresh under the same limit, and if the block exhausts that allowance itself, that error replaces the pending one. Operations already spent stay spent: whenever the limit error is replaced by the `finally` block's own error, even if a `catch` then handles it, or by a `return`, `break` or `continue` leaving the block, the script carries on without a fresh allowance of operations.

When the `finally` block completes, the outcome of the statement it belongs to stands: a value that was produced is still produced, an error that was not handled is still raised, and a `return`, `break` or `continue` that was leaving still leaves. The value of the `finally` block itself is not used, and adding a `finally` block does not change the value the statement produces compared with the same statement without one. If the `finally` block itself raises an error or leaves by `return`, `break` or `continue`, that replaces whichever of those was pending.

`finally` is a keyword of the language, not an identifier.

Scripts that use it produce the same results and errors whether they are evaluated directly or compiled to Grain bytecode and run on the Grain VM. When compiled to Grain, such a script reports no residual fragments and no unsupported construct.

records.summary: The description is concise, direct, and retains the non-obvious behaviors exercised by the tests without unnecessary scaffolding.
records.description:
Make a range usable wherever the language accepts a sequence container. `len(r)` reports how many values the range produces, `r[i]` returns the value at position `i`, `r[i:j]` produces the values from position `i` up to position `j`, `v in r` reports whether `v` is one of the values the range produces, `r.count(v)` reports how many of those values are equal to `v`, `r.index(v)` reports the position of the first of them (`-1` when there is none), `r.reduce(initial, fn)` folds the values as a list does, and `sorted(r)` returns those values in ascending order. A byte or a float equal to a value the range produces is one of them. Slicing a range yields a range. Assigning to a position of a range is not supported.

Every one of these except `sorted` and `reduce` is computed rather than produced: a range spanning 10^15 values answers all of them without producing its values. When a range produces more values than an integer can count, `len(r)` reports the largest representable integer, as does `r.index(v)` for a position past it, while indexing, membership and counting stay defined over every value the range produces.

records.summary: The task is precise and comprehensive; only a couple of dense, test-pinned sentences would benefit from clearer prose.
records.description:
jd records one unchanged element on each side of every list hunk, and the amount is fixed.

Make it configurable with a `context` option.

The option is available globally, as a path-option payload through the option syntax that already exists, and as a command-line flag:

    jd -opts='[{"context":2}]' a.json b.json
    jd -opts='[{"@":["items"],"^":[{"context":0}]}]' a.json b.json
    jd -context=2 a.json b.json

and in Go as `jd.Context(n int) jd.Option`, so `jd.PathOption(jd.Path{jd.PathKey("items")}, jd.Context(2))`.

Required behaviour:

- With `context` set to N, a list hunk records up to N unchanged elements before it and up to N after it. Only arrays compared as lists are affected. A path-scoped setting applies to the array it names and to no other, not even arrays nested inside it, and it governs there whichever order the two settings are given in; a global setting applies everywhere else, and governs every array when the scoped path names no array at all, such as the root of an object.

- `N = 0` means a hunk records nothing around itself: no neighbouring elements on either side, and no start-of-array or end-of-array marker either, not even for a hunk that sits at the very start or the very end of the array.

- A window that reaches the real start or end of its array before it has N elements carries jd's existing start-of-array or end-of-array marker. A window with N or more elements available carries none. A window cut short by an earlier change carries none either, because the array has not ended there.

- Hunks are recorded and applied in order, and two changes always stay two hunks. A window never reaches back to or past an element an earlier hunk changed. The one exception is the element immediately before a hunk, which is always recorded when N is at least 1. It is recorded as the document holds it once the earlier hunks have applied, so if an earlier hunk changed that element, or changed something nested inside it, the value recorded is the one it has after that hunk.

- An element no hunk changes belongs to both windows when it sits between two hunks: a window stops where another hunk changes something, not where another hunk merely names it as context. A removal cuts the next window at the element it removed, wherever in the array that element sat, exactly as a replacement does. The context a hunk records belongs to the array that hunk changes, and never to another.

- The default is unchanged: with the option absent, every diff jd produces is byte-identical to the one it produces today. Setting the option to 1 records one element on each side as today does, except where today names an element another hunk changes, which the window rule above governs. An element whose diffing another option has turned off is accounted for as jd accounts for it today, whatever the setting, including where that leaves a hunk recording a value the document does not hold: this option sets how much context is recorded, not how a suppressed element is counted. Whatever the setting, a diff is written in jd's existing format, and only the number of recorded elements changes. `context` is spelled `{"context":N}` in a diff's option header, and the header appears whenever a diff is rendered together with the options that produced it, whatever amount they carry.

- The recorded context is part of the diff and is still checked when the diff is applied: patching fails when the document does not match the context the diff recorded, and a diff that is rendered and read back again applies exactly as the original did.

- Translating a diff to RFC 6902 keeps it usable by jd: reading that patch back and applying it to the document the diff was taken from produces the same result as the diff itself, and every test operation the patch carries is true of that document. RFC 7386 merge output is unaffected by the option.

- A context that is not a non-negative whole number is rejected when the options are validated, rather than being silently adjusted. Being a whole number is a property of the value and not of how it is written, so `2`, `2.0` and `2e0` all mean two. A value such as `1.00000000000000001` is not a whole number and is rejected even though the nearest binary floating-point double to it is one: decide from the number as written rather than from a float64 conversion.

- The largest whole number a Go `int` can hold is a valid amount and simply records everything the array has. An amount too large for that type is rejected rather than wrapped, and no amount may overflow the arithmetic that builds the window. An options payload must hold nothing but the options: anything after them is an error. Every route that carries a setting refuses an invalid one, a diff's own header included, and a header carries a setting inside a path scope just as the option payload does.

records.description:
jd records one unchanged element on each side of every ordered-list hunk. Make that amount configurable with a `context` option. This feature does not change jd's existing list matching or which changes belong to a hunk; it only changes how many immediately adjacent unchanged elements are recorded.

Expose global context through JSON options such as `[{"context":2}]`, a `-context=N` flag, and `jd.Context(n int) jd.Option`. Passing `Context(N)` to `a.Diff(b, options...)` configures window generation. Path-scoped context uses `jd.PathOption(jd.Path{jd.PathKey("items")}, jd.Context(n))` or the corresponding JSON form `[{"@":["items"],"^":[{"context":N}]}]`; the flag is global-only. The `jd` executable accepts `jd -context=N A.json B.json`, with the flag before its two input paths. Separately, passing options to `Diff.Render(options...)` writes one native `^ ` header per supplied option, in caller order, before the hunks: `^ {"context":N}` for a global option and `^ {"@":["items"],"^":[{"context":N}]}` for the path example.

For example, diffing `[0,1,2,3,4]` to `[0,1,9,3,4]` with `Context(2)` and calling `Render(Context(2))` produces:

```text
^ {"context":2}
@ [2]
  0
  1
- 2
+ 9
  3
  4
```

Required behavior:

- With context N, each ordered-list hunk records up to N immediately neighboring unchanged elements before and after the changed run. A window stops at another change. The same unchanged element may appear in the windows of two neighboring hunks.

- Context zero records no neighboring elements. Whether a side at a real list boundary retains a boundary marker at context zero is unspecified. For positive context, a window that reaches the real start of its list before collecting N elements places a standalone `[` as the first hunk-body line; reaching the real end places a standalone `]` as the last line. A window that collects N elements, or stops at another change, carries no marker.

- Without the option, use depth one and emit no `context` option header. Explicit context one follows the configurable-window rules above; it need not reproduce every historical default rendering byte-for-byte.

- A global setting applies to an ordered list at the document root or stored directly in a top-level object member. A path-scoped setting that names one top-level object member applies only to the ordered list at that exact path and overrides a global setting there regardless of option order. Among settings at the same scope, the last wins. Other such lists keep the global setting, or the default when no global setting exists. Ordered lists nested more deeply are outside this task.

- The unchanged values recorded as context are assertions: applying the diff compares them with the source at those positions and returns an error on a mismatch. Rendering with global or path-scoped options and then reading the native diff preserves those settings and patch behavior; callers do not resupply them when applying the re-read diff.

- Interactions between `context` and `DIFF_ON`, `DIFF_OFF`, `SET`, or `MULTISET` are outside this task. Context-specific RFC 6902 behavior is also outside this task. RFC 7386 behavior remains unchanged.

- Context must be a non-negative integer. `jd.Context(-1)` may construct an option, but `jd.ValidateOptions` must reject it; the JSON option parser likewise rejects invalid or negative values. JSON options need only accept integer literals such as 0, 1, and 2. The command-line flag accepts canonical non-negative base-10 integers. For the web presenter, the fourth argument to `Presenter.UpdateState(ModeDiff, FormatJSON, DiffFormatJd, optionsJSON)` accepts the same JSON option array and applies it to diff generation; presenter output need not include an option header. Malformed native-header values and invalid presenter input are outside this task.

records.description:
Plush templates cannot ask whether a value appears in a collection: `in` is
recognised only as the separator inside a `for` header. Add a membership
operator so a template can test that directly, in both directions.

```plush
<%= "admin" in user.Roles %>
<%= if (id not in allowed) { %>denied<% } %>
<%= for (_, tag) in tags { %><%= tag in featured %><% } %>
```

`left in right` evaluates to `true` or `false`, and `left not in right` is its
negation. Both bind at the same precedence as `==`, so `a + 1 in list` tests
the sum, and `x in list == true` compares the membership result.

The right operand decides what is searched:

- a slice or array: true when one of its elements equals `left`. A template
  array literal (`[1, 2]`) and a Go slice or array taken from the context behave
  alike.
- a map: true when one of its **keys** equals `left`; values are not searched. A
  template hash literal and a Go map taken from the context behave alike, each
  searched by the keys it holds: a literal holds each key in its rendered form,
  so `{1: "a"}` is keyed by `"1"`, while a Go map keeps its own key type.
- a string: true when `left`, rendered as a string, occurs inside it. The empty
  string occurs in every string.
- a `plush.Iterator`: true when one of the values it produces equals `left`.
  Values are read only until a match is found.

A non-nil pointer to a searchable value is searched as the value it points to,
the way `for` already iterates a pointer to a slice.

An element or key equals `left` under the same rules the `==` operator applies
to that same pair of values, so `1 in [1.0]` is true. A pair that `==` rejects
as incomparable is not a match rather than a failure: `1 in ["1"]` is false,
while `1 in ["1", 1]` is true. Slices, maps and structs compare structurally,
so `[1] in [[1], [2]]` is true and a struct value is a member of a slice
holding an equal one, whichever renderer is used.

Any other right operand cannot be searched, and rendering fails with an error.
That holds for `not in` as well, which reports the same failure instead of
negating it into a `true`.

Searching costs render budget, like every other work-producing construct here:
each element, key or iterator value examined costs one loop iteration
(`BudgetCosts.LoopIteration`), and searching a string costs one. A search that
stops early charges only what it examined, and a search that runs past the
remaining budget fails the render the way an over-long loop does.

This repository renders templates through two independently written engines, the
default tree-walking interpreter and the compiled VM renderer, and its own
documentation states that the fast render planner "only handles syntax it can
render with the same behavior as the normal renderer" (README.md:833-849), a
contract its `Test_Parity_*` suite already enforces. `in` must behave
identically under either renderer.

`for (k, v) in list` keeps iterating exactly as it does today, and `not` is the
negation marker only directly in front of `in`: a template may still bind and
read an ordinary value named `not`, including as the left operand of the
operator itself.

Out of scope, each keeping whatever the surrounding expression does with it
today: an operand that is nil or names a value the context does not hold; a
hash-literal key written as an expression (`{1 + 1: "a"}`), which the two
renderers already key differently; and new built-in helpers.

records.label: exp18-numscript-arith
records.summary: Clear, compact task description that preserves the test-pinned arithmetic, parsing, error, and precedence requirements without unnecessary scaffolding.
records.description:
Numscript can add and subtract, but it cannot multiply or divide. Add the `*` and `/` operators to the transaction language.

The language has three numeric-ish value types: a number, a monetary amount (an asset plus a number), and a portion (a ratio written like `60%` or `1/3`). A number is a whole number of unlimited size and may be negative; there is no fractional number. A slash-form portion such as `1/3` is a single portion literal, written with at most one space on each side of the slash, and introducing `/` as an operator must not change which spellings it accepts nor turn one into a division. The new operators are defined over them as follows.

`number * number` produces a number, the exact product.

`monetary * number` produces a monetary amount in the same asset, with the amount multiplied exactly. The operator is commutative: `number * monetary` means the same thing, so `[EUR 10] * 3` and `3 * [EUR 10]` both produce `[EUR 30]`.

`monetary * monetary` is invalid and fails at compile time. It fails the same way the language already fails when `+` or `-` is given operand types it cannot combine.

`portion * number` produces a portion. A portion is valid only from `0%` to `100%` inclusive, so a product outside that range is rejected when the script runs. `portion * portion` produces a portion and is always valid.

`monetary * portion` applies the ratio to the amount and produces a monetary amount in the same asset. An amount is a whole number of units, so when the ratio does not divide the amount evenly the result is rounded down, towards minus infinity. Unlike `monetary * number`, this pairing is not commutative: the amount must be on the left, and `portion * monetary` fails.

`monetary / number` produces a monetary amount in the same asset, truncating towards zero. Dividing by zero fails with a script error rather than crashing the machine.

`*` and `/` bind more tightly than `+` and `-`, so `1 + 2 * 3` is `7` and `2 * 3 + 4 * 5` is `26`. Operators of equal precedence group left to right.

Every other operand combination keeps failing exactly as it does today, including an account, an asset or a string on either side. An operand pairing the new operators do not accept is rejected at compile time, in whichever form the language already uses for that kind of arithmetic type error; a failure that depends on a value rather than a type, such as division by zero or a portion out of range, is a script error raised when the script runs.

Out of scope: dividing a number by a number; the `%` remainder operator; operators on monetary values in different assets; and any change to how a transaction's `send` clauses distribute funds.

records.description:
QLExpress can assign to one variable at a time, but it cannot unpack a List or array into several variables in one statement. Add destructuring assignment: `[a, b] = <expr>;`.

The pattern reuses QLExpress's own list-literal bracket syntax: a bracketed, comma-separated list of targets on the left of `=`, tolerating a trailing comma wherever a list literal does. Each target is either a plain identifier or a nested bracketed pattern, so patterns may nest to any depth: `[a, [b, c]] = [1, [2, 3]];`. A pattern may also have no targets at all, and `[] = <expr>;` then binds nothing. A destructuring assignment is a statement, and it is accepted wherever QLExpress already parses a statement.

Every value a bracketed pattern unpacks must be a `List` or a Java array - the right-hand side for the outermost pattern, and the element it receives for a nested one - including when the pattern has no targets. Such a value is unpacked positionally, element 0 to the first target, element 1 to the second, and so on, with a nested target unpacking the element at its own position. An identifier that appears as a target more than once ends up holding the element of its last occurrence. Any other value is rejected at script-run time with a `QLRuntimeException` carrying the new error code `INVALID_DESTRUCTURE_SOURCE`, whose message contains the phrase `List or array` and the name of the type actually given (or `null`).

If a value being unpacked has fewer elements than its pattern has targets, running the script fails with the error code `INDEX_OUT_BOUND`. If it has more elements than the pattern has targets, the extra elements are silently ignored. Targets are bound one at a time in pattern order as the elements are consumed, so a destructuring assignment that fails part-way through leaves the targets bound before the failure holding the values they were given.

Destructuring assignment is not limited to direct execution. Every runner path that already handles a plain assignment statement must handle this one the same way, reporting and reproducing it just as it does the statements it sits among, including the way a configured `OperatorCheckStrategy` governs a plain assignment's `=` - in both the allowing and the rejecting direction.

The runner's out-variable analysis must treat a destructuring target exactly as it already treats a plain assignment target: a variable that a script destructures into, at any nesting depth, is not reported as externally required, while a variable that is only read - including one referenced by the destructuring source expression itself - is still reported.

records.summary: The description is direct, technically precise, and keeps its detailed requirements aligned with the tested behavior.
records.description:
Dyon has no bitwise operators. Add three: `&` (bitwise AND), `~` (bitwise XOR), and `bor` (bitwise OR). `|` stays the `norm` delimiter in `|x|` and is not an OR token, so OR is the keyword `bor`.

Dyon's only number type is `f64`; there is no integer type. All three operators convert each operand to an integer with a plain `as` cast, apply the bitwise operation, then convert back: an `f64` operand through `i64`, and a `vec4` or `mat4` component through `i32`. Every one of these conversions truncates toward zero, converts `NaN` to `0`, and saturates a magnitude beyond the target type's range to the nearest bound of that range. So `6.7 & 3.2` is `6 & 3`, which is `2`; `(0.0 / 0.0) & 3` is `0`; and `(1.0 / 0.0) & 3` is `3`. Negative operands use two's-complement representation, so `(-6) & 3` is `2`.

The operators are defined over this value-type matrix: `f64,f64`; `vec4,vec4` component-wise; `vec4,f64` and `f64,vec4` as a commutative scalar broadcast; `mat4,mat4` component-wise; `mat4,f64` and `f64,mat4` as a commutative broadcast; and `bool,bool`, where `&` is boolean AND, `~` is boolean XOR (not-equal), and `bor` is boolean OR. In a `vec4` or `mat4` scalar broadcast the `f64` scalar is converted at the component's `i32` width, not through `i64`.

Unlike the short-circuit `&&`/`||`, these are ordinary eager function calls: both operands are always evaluated, so a `false` left operand of `&` does not protect a failing right operand from running.

`&` and `~` bind at the same tier as `*`, `/`, `%`, and `&&`, tighter than `+`/`-`, so `1 + 2 & 3` means `1 + (2 & 3)`, which is `3`. `bor` binds at the tier of `+`, `-`, and `||`, looser than `&`/`~`, so `2 & 3 bor 1` means `(2 & 3) bor 1`, which is `3`. Operators sharing a tier associate left: `6 & 3 ~ 5` is `(6 & 3) ~ 5`, and `1 bor 2 + 3` is `(1 bor 2) + 3`. Sharing `*`'s tier, `&`/`~` inherit the grammar's existing unary-minus scoping there: a leading `-` negates the whole multiplicative chain that follows, not just the next value, so `-6 & 3` means `-(6 & 3)`, which is `-2`, not `(-6) & 3`. Write `(-6) & 3` to negate only the left operand.

Every operand pairing outside this matrix (for example `str & str`, or `mat4 bor vec4`) is rejected at compile time by Dyon's own type checker, using the same generic `Type mismatch (#230)` message every other binary operator here already produces for a type mismatch, naming the operator as `bit_and`, `bit_xor`, or `bit_or`.

Out of scope: bit-shift operators, a unary bitwise-NOT operator, and adding an integer type to the language. The `mat4,vec4` and `vec4,mat4` pairings are also out of scope and must be rejected like any other unsupported pairing.

records.label: exp19-dyon-bitwise
records.summary: The description is direct, technically precise, and keeps its detailed requirements aligned with the tested behavior without spec-style scaffolding.
records.description:
Dyon has no bitwise operators. Add five: `&` (AND), `~` (XOR), `bor` (OR), `<<` and `>>` (shifts). `|` stays the `norm` delimiter in `|x|`, so OR is the keyword `bor`. `xor` and `^` keep their existing power meaning.

Dyon's only number type is `f64`. All five cast each operand to an integer with a plain `as`, apply the operation, then convert back: an `f64` operand through `i64`, and a `vec4` or `mat4` component through `i32`. Each conversion truncates toward zero, converts `NaN` to `0`, and saturates a value beyond the target type's range to that type's minimum or maximum. Negative operands are two's-complement.

`&`, `~`, and `bor` are symmetric and defined over this value-type matrix: `f64,f64`; `vec4,vec4` component-wise; `vec4,f64` and `f64,vec4` as a commutative scalar broadcast; `mat4,mat4` component-wise; `mat4,f64` and `f64,mat4` as a commutative broadcast; and `bool,bool`, where `&` is AND, `~` is XOR (not-equal), and `bor` is OR. A broadcast scalar converts at the component's `i32` width, not through `i64`.

The shifts take the same pairings except `bool,bool`: a count has no boolean meaning. A shift is not symmetric, so its broadcasts are not commutative: the left operand is the value and the right the count, so `f64 << vec4` shifts the scalar by each component and `vec4 << f64` shifts each component by the scalar. A shift resolves at `i64` only when both operands are `f64`; if either is a `vec4` or `mat4`, value, count and result resolve at the component's `i32` width. At whichever of the two widths applies, the count then resolves in this order: a negative count becomes the opposite direction applied to its magnitude, and every later rule reads that effective direction, not the operator as written. A magnitude at or beyond the width saturates rather than wrapping: an effective left shift yields `0`, an effective right shift yields the sign fill, `-1` for a negative value and `0` otherwise. An effective right shift is arithmetic: it preserves the sign of the value it shifts.

Unlike the short-circuit `&&`/`||`, all five are eager: both operands always evaluate.

`&` and `~` bind at the tier of `*`, `/`, `%`, and `&&`, tighter than `+`/`-`. `bor` binds at the tier of `+`, `-`, and `||`. The shifts bind at their own tier, looser than all of those, so either side groups first. Operators sharing a tier associate left. A comparison accepts any of the five unparenthesized on its right, never on its left. On the `*` tier a leading `-` negates the whole multiplicative chain after it, so printing an `&` or `~` keeps every such `-` grouped on either side and the source reloads to the same value.

Every pairing outside an operator's set (for example `str & str` or `true << false`) is rejected at compile time, reusing the existing `Type mismatch (#230)` diagnostic, naming the operator as `bit_and`, `bit_xor`, `bit_or`, `bit_shl`, or `bit_shr`.

Out of scope: unary bitwise-NOT, compound assignment, and an integer type. `mat4,vec4` and `vec4,mat4` are rejected like any unsupported pairing.

records.summary: The task is direct and comprehensive; only two densely phrased, test-pinned rules would benefit from clearer prose.
records.description:
Casbin reads its model files with its own small INI reader in the `config` package. That reader has no idea what a quoted string is: a `#` or `;` anywhere ends the value, and the quotes are stored with it.

Teach the reader to read what the file says.

A quoted stretch runs from a delimiter, `"` or `'`, to the nearest following one of that kind. Everything inside is literal: comment characters, commas, spaces, and a backslash, which escapes only that stretch's own delimiter or another backslash and is otherwise itself. Outside a stretch a backslash protects a comment character, a delimiter, or another backslash the same way, so `a \# b` is one value: a recognized escape stores the character and drops the backslash, and a protected backslash at a line's end does not continue it. Before any other character a backslash is stored unchanged.

A quote wraps a value when it is the first non-space character after the `=`, and wraps a list element when it is first after that element's comma. Its delimiters are removed and nothing else changes, so `"a" "b"` reads as `a "b"`; an element's come off when the elements are read, not in the entry as one string. `""` is the empty value, and as a list one empty element, not an absent one; a key with nothing after its `=` but space or a comment has no elements. A wrapper may also run past its line: every following line belongs to it, including one that looks like a comment or a section header, each break reads as one space, and only its own kind closes it. A backslash ending such a line is content too. A wrapper that never closes is an error naming the line where what it wraps begins.

Quotes occurring after a value has started are retained literally, escapes included. They protect a comment character, and a comma, only when an unescaped quote of the same kind appears later on that same physical line; otherwise they are ordinary text and never an error, leaving the apostrophe in `it's` alone, and a comma after such a quote separates like any other. A matcher like `r.sub == "a#b"` must survive to enforcement, so the comment stripping applied to matchers and effects must respect a stretch too.

A key may be wrapped like a value, may run past its line, and may hold `=` or `#`; a section name may be wrapped but must close inside its own header. For a list value, a comma inside a quoted stretch does not split it, and each element is then read by these same rules. Space around an element is not part of it, and every other comma separates, so an element with nothing left in it is an empty string.

These rules read files. A value a caller hands to `Set` or `AddConfig` is not a line of a file and is never parsed by them: it is stored exactly as given, so reading it back as a string returns those bytes and as a list splits them on every comma.

Also preserve these reader behaviors. Whether a line continues is decided by its last character that is not a space, as read and before any comment is taken off: `v = a \ # remark` ends there, keeping the backslash, while a line whose last character is a backslash continues even when that backslash falls inside a comment. A continued line outside any wrapper drops its backslash and joins the next with one space, ignoring that line's indentation. Inside a wrapper nothing is trimmed: spaces before a break and indentation after it are content, and the break adds its own space. Space between the `=` and a value, and after the value's last character, is not part of it, while space within the value, or between a removed wrapper and what follows, is. A line longer than the reader's buffer is one line, not several. A comment line between two backslash-continued lines is a remark, not its end; a blank line ends it. A header may carry a comment. When an entry has no `=`, the error names the line it started on and reports the entry's text with its escapes resolved and no quoting of its own; where it was gathered from continued lines, that text is the whole assembled entry.

Finally, match section and key names case-insensitively, whatever casing the file or lookup uses.

records.description:
Make `PathOption` establish a comparison-option scope for the matched value and its entire subtree.

A path option's payload applies at the value named by its path and remains active while diffing or comparing every descendant object member and array element. A `PathOption` inside that payload uses a path relative to the matched value, so scopes can be nested to arbitrary depth. Options on unrelated branches must not leak into one another.

For this task, paths contain exact `PathKey("name")` object-member segments and zero-based `PathIndex(i)` array-element segments. Consecutive segments traverse that exact sequence; wildcards and other path element kinds are outside scope. Once a parent scope matches, every descendant inherits it without an array wildcard. During list alignment, a `PathIndex` scope remains anchored to that element's index in the left-hand input.

The inheritable comparison options are `SET`, `MULTISET`, `SetKeys(...)`, `Precision(...)`, `DIFF_ON`, and `DIFF_OFF`. `MERGE`, rendering options, and patch serialization are outside this change.

`SET` ignores order and duplicates; `MULTISET` ignores order but counts duplicates. Because unkeyed members have no positional identity, nested visibility inside these modes is defined only for object members selected by `PathKey`; `PathIndex` visibility into member arrays is outside scope.

`SetKeys("id", "kind")` at an object array uses those values in order as composite identity, then compares matches recursively.

`Precision(p)` considers two numbers equal when their absolute difference is at most `p`.

`DIFF_OFF` suppresses both diff output and equality failure for changes in its active scope. A nested `DIFF_ON` makes changes observable again only in that nested scope.

Resolve competing options by scope, not by the order in which broader scopes were supplied:

- A more specific matching path overrides a global or less-specific path for the same option family, regardless of argument order.
- At the same path, the last declaration for a family wins.
- `SET`, `MULTISET`, and `SetKeys(...)` form one collection-mode family. `DIFF_ON` and `DIFF_OFF` form one visibility family. Each `Precision(...)` replaces the previous precision value.
- Options from different families compose unless validation declares the combination incompatible.

These rules must be observable consistently through both `JsonNode.Diff` and `JsonNode.Equals`.

`ValidateOptions` statically inspects the declared option tree without consulting input documents, so unmatched paths are validated too. It rejects a negative `Precision` wherever it appears and every declared scope whose effective options combine `Precision` with `SET` or `MULTISET`, whether those options are declared directly or inherited. A conflict in one descendant scope does not invalidate an unrelated sibling scope.

`ReadOptionsString` must support these scoped option forms. Its `@` paths use strings for keys and JSON numbers for indexes. An index is valid when its exact mathematical value is a non-negative integer representable as `PathIndex`. Integral decimal and exponent forms are accepted. Fractional, rounded, and out-of-range forms are rejected. A path scope is `{"@":["outer",0],"^":[...]}`; its `^` array contains the same option forms recursively. Use `{"precision":0.1}` and `{"keys":["id"]}` for valued options, and `"SET"`, `"MULTISET"`, `"DIFF_ON"`, or `"DIFF_OFF"` for named options.

records.description:
# Path-scoped option inheritance

Implement `PathOption` as an inheritable comparison scope. A matching scope applies its payload at the matched value and throughout that subtree. Nested paths are relative to their matched parent. Unrelated branches do not share scopes.

## Paths and precedence

Paths contain exact `PathKey("name")` and zero-based `PathIndex(i)` segments. Consecutive segments traverse that sequence. If a selector cannot match its next segment, that scope is inactive. Previously inherited options still apply. An empty path (`Path{}` or `"@":[]`) scopes the root.

During list alignment, `PathIndex` remains anchored to the left-hand input index. It requires a source element and does not activate for a pure addition.

The inheritable families are collection mode (`SET`, `MULTISET`, `SetKeys(...)`), numeric precision (`Precision(...)`), and visibility (`DIFF_ON`, `DIFF_OFF`).

Precedence is:
- a matching specific path beats a broader scope, regardless of declaration order;
- within one scope, the last option in a family wins;
- different families compose unless validation rejects the combination.

## Collection and visibility behavior

`SET`, `MULTISET`, and `SetKeys` share one collection-mode family, so the last declaration at a scope wins. `SET` ignores order and duplicate multiplicity; `MULTISET` preserves multiplicity.

`Precision(p)` treats numeric nodes as equal when their absolute difference is at most `p`; it does not affect non-numbers. `SetKeys("id", "kind")` selects keyed unordered-set mode, pairing objects by those exact values in declaration order, then comparing full matched objects under inherited scopes. Non-objects use exact full-value identity. For each object, use the declared key values present on that object, in declaration order. If none are present, use its exact full-object identity. Duplicate composite identities are outside scope.

For unkeyed `SET` and `MULTISET`, relative `PathKey` scopes apply while comparing object members. Positional visibility scopes inside member arrays are outside scope.

A `PathKey` applies when that member exists on either side. Unpaired members honor inherited `DIFF_ON` and `DIFF_OFF`.

`DIFF_OFF` suppresses both diff output and equality failure. Nested `DIFF_ON` restores visibility only inside its scope.

## Input and validation

Direct construction may use `PathOption(Path{PathKey("outer"), PathIndex(0)}, payload...)` or `NewOption(map[string]any{"@": []any{"outer", 0}, "^": []any{payload...}})`.

Direct precision values may be `json.Number`, `float64`, or `int`. Path segments may be strings or non-negative integral `float64` or `int` values. Reject negative, fractional, non-finite, and above-host-maximum indexes.

`ValidateOptions` inspects the entire declared tree, including unmatched paths. It rejects negative or non-finite precision. It also rejects any effective scope combining precision with `SET` or `MULTISET`, including inherited combinations. A conflict does not invalidate an unrelated sibling.

`ReadOptionsString` uses strings for keys and exact JSON numbers for indexes. Accept integral decimal and exponent forms representable as `PathIndex`; reject fractional, rounded, and out-of-range forms. A scope is `{"@":["outer",0],"^":[...]}` with recursive option forms. Valued forms include `{"precision":0.1}` and `{"keys":["id"]}`. Named forms are `"SET"`, `"MULTISET"`, `"DIFF_ON"`, and `"DIFF_OFF"`.

comments.quote: Everything else about a macro is unchanged.
comments.suggestion: Remove this generic compatibility assurance and keep the following concrete scope rules, which already state the relevant preserved behavior. “Unchanged” is a default expectation and does not add an implementable rule on its own.

records.summary: The description is direct prose with no generated-spec formatting and keeps its detailed requirements aligned with the tested behavior.
records.description:
A QLExpress macro is a named block of statements that is copied into the script wherever the macro is named, so it shares the scope it is used in. It takes no input: a macro body can only read whatever variables happen to exist at the point of use. Give macros parameters.

A macro declaration may carry a parenthesised, comma-separated list of parameter names after its name, as in `macro greet(name) { ... }`.

A macro declared that way is used by naming it with an argument expression per parameter, as a statement of its own, as in `greet("ada");`. A larger expression built around that statement is not a use of the macro; it stays an ordinary expression.

Naming such a macro on its own, as in `greet;`, is a use of it too, supplying no arguments. It is accepted only when every parameter has a default, and rejected like any other call that supplies too few.

Each argument is evaluated once, where the macro is used and in the scope it is used in, and is bound to the matching parameter name for the copied body.

A parameter binding lasts only as long as the expansion. A variable of the same name outside the macro keeps its own value, and the parameter name is gone once the expansion ends.

Everything else about a macro is unchanged. The body still runs in the scope it is expanded into, so a variable it assigns is the caller's variable, and a variable or function it declares is the caller's too.

A declaration that reuses a parameter name is the exception: that name belongs to the expansion, so the declaration goes with it.

A `return`, `break`, or `continue` inside the body still acts on the caller, exactly as one in a macro without parameters does.

The parameters are the one thing that must not outlive the expansion. Wherever such a jump carries control out of the body, including a `break` that ends a surrounding `switch` case, the parameter names go with it. A function declared by the body is the ordinary exception: like any closure it keeps reading the values it captured, parameters included.

A macro declared without a parameter list keeps behaving exactly as it does today, including being used by naming it alone. Only a macro declared with a parameter list is used by naming it with arguments, so an ordinary call that happens to share a parameterless macro's name is still the call it was.

A parameter may declare a default, written after its name as `= expression`, as in `macro greet(name, greeting = "hello") { ... }`. A call that leaves that argument out uses the default instead.

A default is evaluated where the macro is used and in the scope it is used in, so it reads the caller's variables as they stand at that point. It may also read the parameters declared before it.

A default is evaluated only for an expansion that needs it, once per such expansion, and never when the call supplies that argument.

Only trailing parameters may declare defaults: a parameter without a default may not follow one that has a default.

A call must supply at least the parameters that have no default, and at most the whole list. Any other number of arguments is rejected.

A parameter may declare a type before its name, as a function parameter may, as in `macro greet(String name, int times = 1) { ... }`. Enforce a declared type on whatever the expansion binds to that parameter, an argument and a default alike. A value that does not fit the declared type fails that binding, exactly as it does for any other declared variable in this language.

Declaring the same parameter name twice in one macro is rejected, and so is a default on a parameter that is not trailing. Both are reported before any part of the script runs, as the same kind of error the language already raises for a malformed script.

A macro may be used earlier in the same block than the statement that declares it, as a function may.

If a selector cannot match its next segment, that scope is inactive while previously inherited options still apply. An empty path (`Path{}` or `"@":[]`) scopes the root. During list alignment, `PathIndex` remains anchored to the left-hand input index, requires a source element, and does not activate for a pure addition.

The inheritable families are collection mode (`SET`, `MULTISET`, `SetKeys(...)`), numeric precision (`Precision(...)`), and visibility (`DIFF_ON`, `DIFF_OFF`). A matching specific path beats a broader scope regardless of declaration order. Within one scope, the last option in a family wins; separate `PathOption` declarations targeting the same effective path constitute one scope and use that declaration order. Different families compose unless validation rejects the combination.

records.description:
Numbat functions can define local values in a `where` block, but not local functions. Allow `fn` definitions inside a function's `where` block, interleaved with value bindings, for example:

```
fn scale(x: Scalar) -> Scalar = apply(3)
  where gain = 2
    and fn apply(n: Scalar) -> Scalar = n * x * gain
```

A local function body may use the enclosing function's parameters and any value bound earlier in the same `where` block. These values belong to the enclosing call: separate calls of the enclosing function, including several calls in one expression, each see their own values.

Bindings are visible in source order. A local function may call a local function defined earlier in the block, and a later `where` value may call an earlier local function. A local function may be bound to a later `where` value and called through that name, still seeing the values of the call it was defined in.

A local function may call itself recursively. Wherever a local function is visible, its name refers to the local function even when a top-level function has the same name.

A local function's parameter may reuse the name of an enclosing parameter; inside the local function the parameter wins. Like parameters and `where` values, a local function may reuse the name of a unit (for example `g`); wherever the local function is visible, the name refers to the local function.

Local functions accept the same parameter annotations, return annotations and generic `<T: Dim>` parameters as top-level functions. A generic local function can be called at different dimensions in the same expression, each call typed independently.

Errors keep Numbat's existing messages. Using a `where` value that is bound later in the block reports `Unknown identifier '<name>'`. Calling a local function with an argument of the wrong dimension reports the same error as the equivalent top-level call, whose message includes `argument type: <dimension>` (for example `argument type: Time`). A local function is not visible outside its enclosing function: using its name at top level is an error whose message contains that name.

Pretty-printing a function that has local functions produces source that Numbat accepts again and that behaves the same.

Top-level functions, modules and existing `where` value bindings keep their current behavior. Out of scope: anonymous function syntax, local functions outside a function's `where` block, and any change to dimension checking rules.

records.description:
Implement `PathOption` as an inheritable comparison scope. A matching scope applies its payload at the matched value and throughout that subtree. Nested paths are relative to their matched parent, and unrelated branches do not share scopes. Every comparison no scope reaches keeps the behavior it has today, including the existing unordered, keyed, and refinement paths.

Scope paths are sequences of exact `PathKey("name")` segments; consecutive segments traverse that sequence. If a selector cannot match its next segment, that scope is inactive while previously inherited options still apply. An empty path (`Path{}` or `"@":[]`) scopes the root. A scope path containing a `PathIndex` segment is outside scope, and so is a `SetKeys` payload inside a scope. A top-level `SetKeys` keeps the behavior it has today. Existing path forms also keep their meaning beside any scope: `PathOption(Path{PathKey("other"), PathSet{}})` with no payload still compares `other` as a set, and a trailing `PathMultiset{}` still compares it as a multiset.

The inheritable families are collection mode (`SET`, `MULTISET`), numeric precision (`Precision(...)`), and visibility (`DIFF_ON`, `DIFF_OFF`). A matching specific path beats a broader scope regardless of declaration order. Within one scope, the last option in a family wins; separate `PathOption` declarations targeting the same effective path constitute one scope and use that declaration order. Different families compose unless validation rejects the combination.

`SET` and `MULTISET` ignore order; `SET` also ignores duplicate multiplicity, while `MULTISET` preserves counts. `Precision(p)` treats numeric nodes as equal when their absolute difference is at most `p` and does not affect non-numbers.

For `SET` and `MULTISET`, relative `PathKey` scopes carrying a collection mode or precision apply while comparing members. Members that differ only where such a scope relaxes the difference are one member. One member may be backed by several literal copies. Patching locates a member the same way it was compared, so removing or changing it reaches every copy: a source holding two copies patches to a collection holding none. Patching a `SET` or `MULTISET` whose members hold a scoped collection mode other than its own is outside scope. Equally valid matching correspondences need not have identical diff layouts.

A `DIFF_OFF` carried by a `PathOption` suppresses both diff output and equality failure throughout its scope. A nested `DIFF_ON` restores both inside its own scope, and only there. A top-level `DIFF_OFF` keeps the behavior it has today. A `PathKey` scope applies when that key exists on either side, so a key held by just one side follows the visibility at its own path. A visibility scope covering a whole `SET` or `MULTISET` applies to it, but a `DIFF_ON` or `DIFF_OFF` scope that descends into its members is outside scope. Within a suppressed scope, including at the scoped value itself, a replacement by a different kind of value is outside scope. A `DIFF_ON` declared at a key held by just one side exposes that key; whether a `DIFF_ON` declared deeper inside such a one-sided value, and not at the key itself, exposes it is outside scope.

A diff is applied under the options that produced it. Patching the source with such a diff yields a value equal to the target under those same options, both when the diff is applied directly and when it is rendered under those options and read back first. Patching with a diff rendered without its options is outside scope.

Direct construction may use `PathOption(Path{PathKey("outer"), PathKey("inner")}, payload...)` or `NewOption(map[string]any{"@": []any{"outer", "inner"}, "^": []any{payload...}})`. Direct precision values may be `json.Number`, `float64`, or `int`.

`ValidateOptions` inspects the entire declared tree, including unmatched paths. It rejects negative or non-finite precision and any effective scope combining precision with `SET` or `MULTISET`, including inherited combinations. Options in unrelated sibling branches never combine into a conflict, but one conflicting effective scope anywhere makes the whole call return an error.

`ReadOptionsString` reads a scope as `{"@":["outer","inner"],"^":[...]}` with recursive option forms. Valued forms include `{"precision":0.1}`, and `{"keys":["id"]}` at the top level; named forms are `"SET"`, `"MULTISET"`, `"DIFF_ON"`, and `"DIFF_OFF"`.

records.label: exp45-numbat-tuples
records.summary: The description is direct, compact, and specifies the new language behavior without generated-spec scaffolding or unnecessary implementation direction.
records.description:
Numbat has lists and named structs but no way to group a fixed number of values of different types without declaring a struct. Add tuples.

A tuple literal is a parenthesized, comma-separated list of two or more expressions, for example `(2 m, 3 s, true)`. A trailing comma is allowed. A single parenthesized expression such as `(x)` is still just grouping, not a tuple. Tuples are displayed like their literal, for example `(2 m, 3 s, true)`. Inside string interpolation, a tuple is inserted the same way a list is.

Elements are read by position with `t.0`, `t.1` and so on, so `t.1.0` reads a nested tuple. The period may follow a name, a call, a parenthesized expression or tuple literal, or another element access. As with struct fields, whitespace may come before the period. Element types, including dimensions, are kept. Element access works whenever the value is a tuple, including when its tuple type is only determined by type inference, such as the result of a generic function. A function parameter used with element access needs a type annotation; without one, the program is rejected.

A tuple type is written `(Type1, Type2, ...)` wherever a type annotation is accepted, including parameters, return types, struct fields, `List<...>`, and inside other tuples. Parenthesized dimension expressions such as `(Length / Time)^2` keep working as types. A value matches a tuple type when it is a tuple of the same length whose element types match; any other value is rejected like any other type mismatch. Generic type and dimension parameters may appear inside tuple types. One-element tuples do not exist, so `(x,)` is rejected as an expression and `(T,)` as a type.

`==` and `!=` compare tuples element by element, the same way lists are compared. Comparing tuples whose element types differ is rejected with Numbat's usual `Incompatible types in comparison` error, and a list whose elements are tuples of different shapes gives the usual `Incompatible types in list` error.

Errors:

- Reading an element past the end of a tuple is a type error whose message contains `Element <n> does not exist in tuple type`.
- Reading an element of a value that is not a tuple is a type error whose message contains `Can not access element <n> of non-tuple type`.

These messages are required where the operand types are known without inference. When a mismatch only becomes visible through type inference, for example on results of generic functions, the program must still be rejected, but the message is not specified.

Pretty-printing a tuple literal or a tuple type produces source that Numbat accepts again with the same meaning. Element access is pretty-printed the way struct field access is. Out of scope: tuple destructuring, the empty tuple, and unit conversion of tuples with `->`.

records.label: exp44-numbat-local-functions
records.summary: The description is concise, direct, and keeps its detailed behavioral requirements aligned with the tested surface.
records.description:
Numbat functions can define local values in a `where` block, but not local functions. Allow `fn` definitions inside a function's `where` block, interleaved with value bindings, for example:

```
fn scale(x: Scalar) -> Scalar = apply(3)
  where gain = 2
    and fn apply(n: Scalar) -> Scalar = n * x * gain
```

A local function body may use the enclosing function's parameters and any value bound earlier in the same `where` block. These values belong to the enclosing call: separate calls of the enclosing function, including several calls in one expression, each see their own values.

Bindings are visible in source order. A local function may call a local function defined earlier in the block, and a later `where` value may call an earlier local function. A local function may be bound to a later `where` value and called through that name, still seeing the values of the call it was defined in.

A local function may call itself recursively. Wherever a local function is visible, its name refers to the local function even when a top-level function has the same name. This includes a built-in function such as `sin`. Outside the enclosing function, such a name keeps its top-level meaning.

A local function's parameter may reuse the name of an enclosing parameter; inside the local function the parameter wins. Like parameters and `where` values, a local function may reuse the name of a unit (for example `g`); wherever the local function is visible, the name refers to the local function. Before a local function or `where` value that reuses a unit name, the name still refers to the unit.

Local functions accept the same parameter annotations, return annotations and generic `<T: Dim>` parameters as top-level functions. Their annotations may also use the enclosing function's type parameters. A generic local function can be called at different dimensions in the same expression, each call typed independently.

Errors keep Numbat's existing messages. Using a `where` value that is bound later in the block reports `Unknown identifier '<name>'`. Calling a local function with an argument of the wrong dimension reports the same error as the equivalent top-level call, whose message includes `argument type: <dimension>` (for example `argument type: Time`). A local function is not visible outside its enclosing function: using its name at top level is an error whose message contains that name.

Pretty-printing a function that has local functions produces source that Numbat accepts again and that behaves the same. This includes local functions whose annotations use the enclosing function's type parameters.

Top-level functions, modules and existing `where` value bindings keep their current behavior. Out of scope: anonymous function syntax, local functions outside a function's `where` block, and any change to dimension checking rules. Also out of scope are a local function with the same name as its enclosing function, decorators on a function whose `where` block defines local functions, and pretty-printing when the enclosing function has unannotated parameters.

records.description:
Knex ships a family of JSON `where` predicates for JSON and JSONB columns: `whereJsonObject`, `whereJsonPath`, `whereJsonSupersetOf` and `whereJsonSubsetOf`, each with `or`- and `and`-prefixed variants. The key-existence member of that family was never finished: `whereJsonHasNone` is declared on the query builder but throws a `TypeError` when it is called, and neither `whereJsonHasAll` nor `whereJsonHasAny` exists at all. Finish the family.

Provide `whereJsonHasAll(column, keys)`, `whereJsonHasAny(column, keys)` and a working `whereJsonHasNone(column, keys)`. Provide the prefixed forms as well: `orWhereJsonHasAll` and `andWhereJsonHasAll`, `orWhereJsonHasAny` and `andWhereJsonHasAny`, `orWhereJsonHasNone` and `andWhereJsonHasNone`. Each of the nine must also be callable as the first call on the knex instance itself, `knex.whereJsonHasAll(column, keys)`, and not solely on a builder. The builder's `not` modifier is honoured. `.not.whereJsonHasAll(column, keys)` matches a stored object that lacks at least one of the listed names. `.not.whereJsonHasAny(column, keys)` matches a stored object that has none of them.

`keys` is an array of member names. A single string is accepted as a one-member array.

A member name is a literal key, never a path expression. `whereJsonHasAll('data', ['a.b'])` asks for a member whose name is the three characters `a.b`; it matches `{"a.b": 1}` and does not match `{"a": {"b": 1}}`. The same holds for a name containing a quote, a bracket, an asterisk, a dollar sign or a backslash. A trailing blank is part of a name too, so `w` and `w ` are different members on every supported engine. One of them compares character strings by padding the shorter operand out to the length of the longer, under every collation it offers, so on that engine a comparison that rests on its string equality alone answers for the wrong member.

The three predicates test membership at the top level of the stored value, and the value stored under a member never matters. A member that is present with the JSON value `null` is present. `whereJsonHasAll` matches when every listed name is present. `whereJsonHasAny` matches when at least one is. `whereJsonHasNone` matches when none is. An empty array lists no name, so `whereJsonHasAll` and `whereJsonHasNone` match every stored JSON object and `whereJsonHasAny` matches none.

Only a stored JSON object can satisfy any of the three. A row whose column holds a JSON array, a JSON scalar, SQL `NULL`, or text that is not JSON at all is matched by none of the three predicates, including `whereJsonHasNone`.

Every dialect whose engine can express key existence must compile these predicates into that engine's own idiom, following the per-dialect pattern the existing JSON predicates use. A PostgreSQL column holding these documents may be declared either `json` or `jsonb`, and the predicates answer about the document rather than about the declared type, so both forms of column must be supported even where the engine's own key-existence facilities read just one of them. Redshift is the only supported engine with no facility for it: its client must define the methods and throw when the statement is compiled, exactly as it already does for `whereJsonSupersetOf`.

Each predicate compiles to a condition the engine accepts directly in a `where` clause, not to a value the clause then has to compare. An operator that contains the placeholder character must survive the dialect's own placeholder handling. A PostgreSQL client rewrites the placeholders of a finished statement into positional parameters before sending it, and that rewrite must not corrupt such an operator.

The member names are supplied by the caller, so they travel as bindings rather than as text interpolated into the statement. One supported engine accepts no binding where the member name has to go and requires a literal there. On that engine the name is written into the statement as a quoted literal instead. That literal is escaped. A quote, a backslash or a control character can neither end it early nor change which member is named, and the placeholder character the client positions afterwards stays data inside it.

The package publishes its own TypeScript declarations, and a caller who reaches these predicates through them must see the same surface the runtime offers: every one of the nine methods, accepting either form of the keys argument and returning the builder.

records.summary: The description is technically specific and test-aligned, with only a small amount of awkward phrasing and an unpinned boundary restriction.
records.description:
Implement `PathOption` as an inheritable comparison scope. A matching scope applies its payload at the matched value and throughout that subtree. Nested paths are relative to their matched parent, and unrelated branches do not share scopes. Every comparison no scope reaches keeps the behavior it has today, including the existing unordered, keyed, and refinement paths.

Scope paths are sequences of exact `PathKey("name")` segments; consecutive segments traverse that sequence. If a selector cannot match its next segment, that scope is inactive while previously inherited options still apply. Whether a nested `PathKey` selector still pending at an ordered array matches keys inside that array's elements is outside scope. An empty path (`Path{}` or `"@":[]`) scopes the root. A scope path containing a `PathIndex` segment is outside scope, and so is a `SetKeys` payload inside a scope. A top-level `SetKeys` keeps the behavior it has today. Existing path forms also keep their meaning beside any scope: `PathOption(Path{PathKey("other"), PathSet{}})` with no payload still compares `other` as a set, and a trailing `PathMultiset{}` still compares it as a multiset.

The inheritable families are collection mode (`SET`, `MULTISET`), numeric precision (`Precision(...)`), and visibility (`DIFF_ON`, `DIFF_OFF`). A matching specific path beats a broader scope regardless of declaration order. Within one scope, the last option in a family wins; separate `PathOption` declarations targeting the same effective path constitute one scope and use that declaration order. A nested `PathOption(Path{}, ...)` targets the scope that holds it and takes its place in that scope's declaration order. Different families compose unless validation rejects the combination.

`SET` and `MULTISET` ignore order; `SET` also ignores duplicate multiplicity, while `MULTISET` preserves counts. `Precision(p)` treats numeric nodes as equal when their absolute difference is at most `p` and does not affect non-numbers.

For `SET` and `MULTISET`, relative `PathKey` scopes carrying a collection mode or precision apply while comparing members. Members that differ only where such a scope relaxes the difference are one member. A `MULTISET` whose members match several counterparts through a scoped `Precision` is outside scope. One member may be backed by several literal copies; removing or changing it leaves no copy behind, so a source holding two copies patches to a collection holding none. Patching copies that are one member through a scoped `Precision` is outside scope. Patching a `SET` or `MULTISET` whose members hold a scoped collection mode other than its own is outside scope. Equally valid matching correspondences need not have identical diff layouts.

A `DIFF_OFF` carried by a `PathOption` suppresses both diff output and equality failure throughout its scope. A nested `DIFF_ON` restores both inside its own scope, and only there. A top-level `DIFF_OFF` keeps the behavior it has today, except that a matching specific-path `DIFF_ON` beats it even when declared before it. A `PathKey` scope applies when that key exists on either side, so a key held by just one side follows the visibility at its own path. A visibility scope covering a whole `SET` or `MULTISET` applies to it, but a `DIFF_ON` or `DIFF_OFF` scope that descends into its members is outside scope. Within a suppressed scope, including at the scoped value itself, a replacement by a different kind of value is outside scope. A `DIFF_ON` declared at a key held by just one side exposes that key; a `DIFF_ON` declared deeper inside such a one-sided value is outside scope.

`Patch` stays unchanged: it keeps its signature and reads no options, including any recorded on the diff. Patching the source with a diff produced under some options yields a value equal to the target under those options, both when the diff is applied directly and when it is rendered under those options and read back first. Patching an ordered list compared under a scoped `Precision` is outside scope. Patching with a diff rendered without its options is outside scope.

Direct construction may use `PathOption(Path{PathKey("outer"), PathKey("inner")}, payload...)` or `NewOption(map[string]any{"@": []any{"outer", "inner"}, "^": []any{payload...}})`. Direct precision values may be `json.Number`, `float64`, or `int`.

`ValidateOptions` inspects the entire declared tree, including unmatched paths. It rejects negative or non-finite precision and any effective scope combining precision with `SET` or `MULTISET`, including inherited combinations. Unrelated sibling branches never combine into a conflict, but one conflicting effective scope anywhere makes the whole call return an error.

`ReadOptionsString` reads a scope as `{"@":["outer","inner"],"^":[...]}` with recursive option forms. Valued forms include `{"precision":0.1}`, and `{"keys":["id"]}` at the top level; named forms are `"SET"`, `"MULTISET"`, `"DIFF_ON"`, and `"DIFF_OFF"`.

records.description:
Implement `PathOption` as an inheritable comparison scope. A matching scope applies its payload at the matched value and throughout that subtree. Nested paths are relative to their matched parent, and unrelated branches do not share scopes. Every comparison no scope reaches keeps the behavior it has today, including the existing unordered, keyed, and refinement paths.

Scope paths are sequences of exact `PathKey("name")` segments; consecutive segments traverse that sequence. If a selector cannot match its next segment, that scope is inactive while previously inherited options still apply. Whether a nested `PathKey` selector still pending at an ordered array matches keys inside that array's elements is outside scope. An empty path (`Path{}` or `"@":[]`) scopes the root. A scope path containing a `PathIndex` segment is outside scope, and so is a `SetKeys` payload inside a scope. A top-level `SetKeys` keeps the behavior it has today. Existing path forms also keep their meaning beside any scope: `PathOption(Path{PathKey("other"), PathSet{}})` with no payload still compares `other` as a set, and a trailing `PathMultiset{}` still compares it as a multiset.

The inheritable families are collection mode (`SET`, `MULTISET`), numeric precision (`Precision(...)`), and visibility (`DIFF_ON`, `DIFF_OFF`). A matching specific path beats a broader scope regardless of declaration order. Within one scope, the last option in a family wins; separate `PathOption` declarations targeting the same effective path constitute one scope and use that declaration order. A nested `PathOption(Path{}, ...)` targets the scope that holds it and takes its place in that scope's declaration order. Different families compose unless validation rejects the combination.

`SET` and `MULTISET` ignore order; `SET` also ignores duplicate multiplicity, while `MULTISET` preserves counts. `Precision(p)` treats numeric nodes as equal when their absolute difference is at most `p` and does not affect non-numbers.

For `SET` and `MULTISET`, relative `PathKey` scopes carrying a collection mode or precision apply while comparing members. Members that differ only where such a scope relaxes the difference are one member. A `MULTISET` whose members match several counterparts through a scoped `Precision` is outside scope. One member may be backed by several literal copies; patching a removal or change of such a member is outside scope. Patching a `SET` or `MULTISET` whose members hold a scoped collection mode other than its own is outside scope. Equally valid matching correspondences need not have identical diff layouts.

A `DIFF_OFF` carried by a `PathOption` suppresses both diff output and equality failure throughout its scope. A nested `DIFF_ON` restores both inside its own scope, and only there. A top-level `DIFF_OFF` keeps the diff output it has today, except that a matching specific-path `DIFF_ON` beats it even when declared before it; whether it also suppresses equality failure is outside scope. A `PathKey` scope applies when that key exists on either side, so a key held by just one side follows the visibility at its own path. A visibility scope covering a whole `SET` or `MULTISET` applies to it; one descending into its members is outside scope. A replacement by a different kind of value within a suppressed scope, including at the scoped value, is outside scope. A `DIFF_ON` declared at a key held by just one side exposes that key; one declared deeper inside that value is outside scope.

`Patch` stays unchanged: it keeps its signature and reads no options, including any recorded on the diff. Patching the source with a diff produced under some options yields a value equal to the target under those options, both when the diff is applied directly and when it is rendered under those options and read back first. Patching an ordered list compared under a scoped `Precision` is outside scope. Patching with a diff rendered without its options is outside scope.

Direct construction may use `PathOption(Path{PathKey("outer"), PathKey("inner")}, payload...)` or `NewOption(map[string]any{"@": []any{"outer", "inner"}, "^": []any{payload...}})`. Direct precision values may be `json.Number`, `float64`, or `int`.

`ValidateOptions` inspects the entire declared tree, including unmatched paths; validating options under a path that is not all `PathKey` segments is outside scope. It rejects negative or non-finite precision and any effective scope combining precision with `SET` or `MULTISET`, including inherited combinations. Unrelated sibling branches never combine into a conflict, but one conflicting effective scope anywhere makes the whole call return an error.

`ReadOptionsString` reads a scope as `{"@":["outer","inner"],"^":[...]}` with recursive option forms. Valued forms include `{"precision":0.1}`, and `{"keys":["id"]}` at the top level; named forms are `"SET"`, `"MULTISET"`, `"DIFF_ON"`, and `"DIFF_OFF"`.

records.summary: The description is direct, compact, and maps its behavioral constraints closely to the tested feature surface without spec-style scaffolding.
records.description:
Numbat functions must currently be called with every argument, in parameter order. Add default values for function parameters and named arguments in function calls.

A parameter may declare a default value, as in `fn scale(x: Length, n: Scalar = 2) -> Length = x * n`. Once a parameter has a default, every later parameter must have one too; otherwise the definition is rejected. A call may leave out arguments for parameters that have defaults, so `scale(3 m)` returns `6 m`.

Any argument may be passed by name, as in `scale(3 m, n = 5)` or `scale(n = 5, x = 3 m)`. This works for every function called by its name, including prelude functions. Named arguments follow all positional arguments and may come in any order. A call is rejected if it names an unknown parameter, fills a parameter twice, puts a positional argument after a named one, or leaves a parameter without a default unfilled.

A default must match the type of its parameter, and a mismatch is rejected when the function is defined, before any call. For a parameter without a type annotation, the default determines its type. The default is evaluated again on every call that leaves the argument out.

A default is evaluated in the scope where the function is defined. It can use variables and functions defined before the function, seeing them as the function body does, but not the function's own parameters or `where` values. The caller's parameters and `where` values never affect it. A unit name used in a default keeps its unit meaning even when one of the function's parameters has the same name.

When `f` is a function, `x -> f` and `x |> f` behave like the call `f(x)`, so they also work when all other parameters of `f` have defaults. `x |> f(args)` passes `x` as the last positional argument.

Defaults and named arguments apply only when a function is called directly by its name. A function used as a value, for example stored in a variable or passed to another function, keeps its full parameter list and must be called with all arguments in order.

Every displayed function signature, including the one shown by `info`, shows each default after its parameter's type, as in `n: Scalar = 2`. Pretty-printing a function definition or a function call produces source that Numbat accepts again with the same meaning.

Out of scope: default values for struct fields, named arguments for procedures such as `print` and `assert_eq`, and adding defaults to existing prelude functions.

records.description:
Implement `PathOption` as an inheritable comparison scope. A matching scope applies its payload at the matched value and throughout that subtree. Nested paths are relative to their matched parent, and unrelated branches do not share scopes. Every comparison no scope reaches keeps the behavior it has today, including the existing unordered, keyed, and refinement paths; repeated top-level collection modes still use the first.

Scope paths are sequences of exact `PathKey("name")` segments. If a selector cannot match its next segment, that scope is inactive while previously inherited options still apply. Whether a nested `PathKey` selector still pending at an ordered array matches keys inside that array's elements is outside scope. An empty path (`Path{}` or `"@":[]`) scopes the root. A scope path containing a `PathIndex` segment is outside scope, and so is a `SetKeys` payload inside a scope. A top-level `SetKeys` keeps the behavior it has today. Existing path forms also keep their meaning beside any scope: `PathOption(Path{PathKey("other"), PathSet{}})` with no payload still compares `other` as a set, and a trailing `PathMultiset{}` still compares it as a multiset. That holds even where a broader scope inherits the other collection mode.

The inheritable families are collection mode (`SET`, `MULTISET`) and numeric precision (`Precision(...)`). `DIFF_ON` and `DIFF_OFF` are not inheritable families and keep the behavior they have today. A bare top-level `DIFF_OFF` has no effect when the source root is an array. When the source root is an object, it still reports that object's replacement by a value of another kind. A matching specific path beats a broader scope regardless of declaration order, and a root `PathOption(Path{}, ...)` beats a same-family bare top-level option in either order. Within one scope, the last option in a family wins; separate `PathOption` declarations at one effective path form one scope in declaration order. A nested `PathOption(Path{}, ...)` targets the scope that holds it and takes its place in that scope's declaration order. Different families compose unless validation rejects the combination.

`SET` and `MULTISET` ignore order; `SET` also ignores duplicate multiplicity, while `MULTISET` preserves counts. `Precision(p)` treats numeric nodes as equal when their absolute difference is at most `p` and does not affect non-numbers.

For `SET` and `MULTISET`, relative `PathKey` scopes carrying a collection mode or precision apply while comparing members. Members that differ only where such a scope relaxes the difference are one member. A `MULTISET` whose members match several counterparts through a scoped `Precision` is outside scope. One member may be backed by several literal copies; patching a removal or change of such a member is outside scope. Patching a `SET` or `MULTISET` whose members hold a scoped collection mode other than its own is outside scope. Equally valid matching correspondences need not have identical diff layouts.

`Patch` stays unchanged: it keeps its signature and reads no options, including any recorded on the diff. A diff produced under some options patches the source to a value equal to the target under those options, whether applied directly or rendered under those options and read back first. Patching an ordered list compared under a scoped `Precision` is outside scope. Patching with a diff rendered without its options is outside scope.

Direct construction may use `PathOption(Path{PathKey("outer"), PathKey("inner")}, payload...)` or `NewOption(map[string]any{"@": []any{"outer", "inner"}, "^": []any{payload...}})`. Direct precision values may be `json.Number`, `float64`, or `int`.

`ValidateOptions` inspects the entire declared tree, including unmatched paths. It rejects a negative or non-finite precision wherever declared, including beside a `SetKeys` payload or under a `PathIndex` segment, and any effective key scope combining precision with `SET` or `MULTISET`, including inherited combinations. Unrelated sibling branches never combine into a conflict, but one conflicting effective scope anywhere makes the whole call return an error.

`ReadOptionsString` reads a scope as `{"@":["outer","inner"],"^":[...]}` with recursive option forms. Valued forms include `{"precision":0.1}`, and `{"keys":["id"]}` at the top level; named forms are `"SET"` and `"MULTISET"`.
