records.description:
Numbat functions must currently be called with every argument, in parameter order. Add default values for function parameters and named arguments in function calls.

A parameter may declare a default value, as in `fn scale(x: Length, n: Scalar = 2) -> Length = x * n`. Once a parameter has a default, every later parameter must have one too; otherwise the definition is rejected. A call may leave out arguments for parameters that have defaults, so `scale(3 m)` returns `6 m`.

Any argument may be passed by name, as in `scale(3 m, n = 5)` or `scale(n = 5, x = 3 m)`. This works for every function called by its name, including prelude functions. Named arguments follow all positional arguments and may come in any order. A call is rejected if it names an unknown parameter, fills a parameter twice, puts a positional argument after a named one, or leaves a parameter without a default unfilled.

A default must match the type of its parameter, and a mismatch is rejected when the function is defined, before any call. For a parameter without a type annotation, the default determines its type. The default is evaluated again on every call that leaves the argument out.

A default is evaluated in the scope where the function is defined. It can use variables and functions defined before the function, seeing them as the function body does, but not the function's own parameters or `where` values. The caller's parameters and `where` values never affect it. A unit name used in a default keeps its unit meaning even when one of the function's parameters has the same name.

Defaults and named arguments apply only when a function is called directly by its name. A function used as a value, for example stored in a variable or passed to another function, keeps its full parameter list and must be called with all arguments in order.

Every displayed function signature, including the one shown by `info`, shows each default after its parameter's type, as in `n: Scalar = 2`. Pretty-printing a function definition or a function call produces source that Numbat accepts again with the same meaning.

Out of scope: default values for struct fields, named arguments for procedures such as `print` and `assert_eq`, and adding defaults to existing prelude functions.

records.summary: The description is direct, technically load-bearing, and avoids unnecessary spec scaffolding.
records.description:

- `UUID()` converts to `uuid.UUID`.
- `Integer(*, strict=False)` converts to `int`.
- `Float(*, allow_nan=False)` converts to `float`.
- `Decimal(places=None, rounding=None, *, allow_nan=False)` converts to `decimal.Decimal`.
- `Boolean(*, truthy=None, falsy=None)` converts to `bool`.
- `DateTime(format=None)` converts to `datetime.datetime`; `NaiveDateTime(format=None, *, timezone=None)` and `AwareDateTime(format=None, *, default_timezone=None)` are its naive and aware variants.
- `Date(format=None)` converts to `datetime.date`; `Time(format=None)` converts to `datetime.time`.
- `TimeDelta(precision="seconds")` converts to `datetime.timedelta`.
- `IP(*, version=None)` converts to an `ipaddress` address; `IPInterface(*, version=None)` converts to an `ipaddress` interface.

Each option has the same meaning, default, and construction-time validation as the identically named option of the field with the same name. `format=None` selects the field's default format. `version` is `None`, `4`, or `6`, selecting any address, IPv4 addresses alone, or IPv6 addresses alone. Those three choices match `fields.IP`, `fields.IPv4`, and `fields.IPv6` and their interface counterparts.

Every new class also accepts an `error_messages` mapping as a keyword argument. Its keys and default messages are the same as the `default_error_messages` of the corresponding field. An override for one key keeps the defaults for the others, and messages are interpolated with the same placeholders the field uses.

Calling a validator with a value returns the value exactly as the corresponding field would deserialize it. It raises `marshmallow.ValidationError` carrying the corresponding field's message for exactly the inputs that field rejects.

The fields with the same names as these validators, together with `IPv4`, `IPv6`, `IPv4Interface`, and `IPv6Interface`, obtain their parsing from these validators instead of keeping their own copies of the rules. A field's `error_messages` overrides reach the validator it uses.

Note that a validator instance holds no reference to a field or a schema, so it can be constructed and called on its own, given nothing beyond the options listed above.

Tests are run with `python3 -m pytest tests/` from the repository root.

comments.quote: No class moves module, so a config pickled before this change still loads and compares equal afterwards.
comments.suggestion: Use plain grammatical prose: “Do not move any classes between modules, so configs pickled before this change still load and compare equal afterwards.” This keeps the compatibility requirement but avoids the malformed “moves module” construction.

records.summary: The description is direct and technically specific; nearly all of its detailed requirements are load-bearing under the hidden tests.
records.description:
Extract the merge and conversion algorithms that `omegaconf.basecontainer.BaseContainer` currently carries as private static and instance methods into a new module of plain functions, `omegaconf.container_ops`, and make every existing entry point obtain that behaviour from the new module. This is a behaviour-preserving restructuring: merging and converting configs produce the same values, the same node types and metadata, the same flags, the same parent links, and the same errors as before.

Add the following functions to `omegaconf.container_ops`:

- `merge_into(target, *sources, allow_readonly_target=False)` merges each source into `target` in place, the way `BaseContainer.merge_with` merges today. That includes turning plain dicts, lists, tuples and structured configs into configs, honouring `allow_objects`, and repairing the parent hierarchy at the end. With `allow_readonly_target=True` it may merge into a readonly container or a `TupleConfig`, exactly as the internal merges behind `OmegaConf.merge` and `OmegaConf.unsafe_merge` do today.
- `map_merge(dest, src, allow_readonly_target=False)` merges one `DictConfig` into another.
- `list_merge(dest, src)` merges one `ListConfig` into another.
- `tuple_merge(dest, src)` merges a `ListConfig` or `TupleConfig` into a `TupleConfig`.
- `to_content(conf, resolve, throw_on_missing, enum_to_str=False, structured_config_mode=SCMode.DICT, resolved_node_cache=None, encode_missing_literals=False)` converts a container to its primitive form, the way `OmegaConf.to_container` converts today. Every option keeps the meaning of the same-named option of `OmegaConf.to_container`. `resolved_node_cache` keeps its meaning as the shared cache of resolved nodes for one conversion.

Each function accepts and returns exactly what the corresponding present-day `BaseContainer` method accepts and returns, and raises the same exceptions for the same inputs. Warnings that a merge suppresses today stay suppressed when the merge is performed through `merge_into`.

Every caller of the removed methods obtains merging and conversion from these functions instead of keeping its own copy of the algorithms. That covers `BaseContainer.merge_with`, `OmegaConf.merge`, `OmegaConf.unsafe_merge`, the merge that assigns a structured config into a union-typed node, `OmegaConf.to_container`, and `OmegaConf.to_yaml`. `BaseContainer` no longer defines `_merge_with`, `_map_merge`, `_list_merge`, `_tuple_merge`, or `_to_content`.

`omegaconf.container_ops` defines functions only. It introduces no class, and the method resolution order of `DictConfig`, `ListConfig`, and `TupleConfig` is unchanged. No class moves module, so a config pickled before this change still loads and compares equal afterwards. Importing `omegaconf.container_ops` in a fresh interpreter succeeds. The module does not import `omegaconf.basecontainer`, `omegaconf.dictconfig`, `omegaconf.listconfig`, `omegaconf.tupleconfig`, or `omegaconf.omegaconf` at module level, so the dependency direction runs from the containers to the operations.

Add a one-line news fragment for this change under `news/`, following the repository's convention.

Tests are run with `python3 -m pytest tests/` from the repository root.

records.description:
Fix generators in this compiler so return and throw work. Right now a generator object has next and nothing else.

Here's what I expect. The injected completion occurs at the suspended `yield`. A thrown completion runs `catch` and `finally` blocks, while a return completion runs only `finally` blocks. If finally yields, stay suspended there; a return inside finally overrides the injected completion. Return before the first next closes the generator without running the body. After completion, `return(value)` must produce `{ value, done: true }`, while `throw(error)` must rethrow the supplied error. A closed generator is exhausted for for-of, spread and destructuring. Re-entering a running generator through next, return or throw throws TypeError.

For yield*: forward return and throw to the delegate if present, forward the next argument to the delegate's next. done:true from a forwarded return finishes the outer generator with that value; done:true from a forwarded throw becomes the yield* value; done:false yields the result and keeps delegating. No return on the delegate: finish the outer generator with the requested value. No throw: call the delegate's return if any, then throw TypeError.

These semantics apply to the default Lua target. Closing an iterator when a `for-of` loop exits early is outside scope.

comments.quote: Extract the merge, conversion, type-hint propagation, and item-assignment algorithms that OmegaConf's container classes currently carry as private methods into a new module of plain functions, `omegaconf.container_ops`.
comments.suggestion: This description is too prescriptive — focus on behavior instead of implementation details. Write your description like how you would prompt an LLM.

records.summary: The description is too prescriptive — focus on behavior instead of implementation details, and write it like how you would prompt an LLM.
records.description:
Extract the merge, conversion, type-hint propagation, and item-assignment algorithms that OmegaConf's container classes currently carry as private methods into a new module of plain functions, `omegaconf.container_ops`. Every existing entry point obtains that behaviour from the new module. This is a behaviour-preserving restructuring: merging, converting, and assigning into configs produce the same values, the same node types and metadata, the same flags, the same parent links, and the same errors as before.

The merge side of the module is `merge_into(target, *sources, allow_readonly_target=False)`, which merges each source into `target` in place the way `BaseContainer.merge_with` merges today. That includes turning plain dicts, lists, tuples and structured configs into configs, honouring `allow_objects`, and repairing the parent hierarchy at the end. With `allow_readonly_target=True` it may merge into a readonly container or a `TupleConfig`, exactly as the internal merges behind `OmegaConf.merge` and `OmegaConf.unsafe_merge` do today. The per-kind merges sit beside it. `map_merge(dest, src, allow_readonly_target=False)` merges one `DictConfig` into another and `list_merge(dest, src)` merges one `ListConfig` into another. `tuple_merge(dest, src)` merges a `ListConfig` or `TupleConfig` into a `TupleConfig`.

Conversion is `to_content(conf, resolve, throw_on_missing, enum_to_str=False, structured_config_mode=SCMode.DICT, resolved_node_cache=None, encode_missing_literals=False)`. It converts a container to its primitive form the way `OmegaConf.to_container` converts today. Every option keeps the meaning of the same-named option of `OmegaConf.to_container`, and `resolved_node_cache` keeps its meaning as the shared cache of resolved nodes for one conversion.

Type-hint propagation and item assignment move the same way. `apply_type_hint(node, type_hint)` makes `node` compatible with `type_hint`, mutating it where needed, and behaves the way the recursive type-hint update `_deep_update_type_hint` in `omegaconf.basecontainer` behaves today. That covers structured-config promotion, element typing for lists, dicts and tuples, union wrapping, and the same validation errors for incompatible values, keys and tuple lengths. `set_item(target, key, value)` stores `value` under `key` in the container `target` the way `BaseContainer._set_item_impl` stores it today. That covers copying a node that already belongs to a tree, readonly and type validation, wrapping a plain value into a node, and propagating the target's type hint into the stored node.

Each function accepts and returns exactly what the corresponding present-day `BaseContainer` method accepts and returns, and raises the same exceptions for the same inputs. Warnings that a merge suppresses today stay suppressed when the merge is performed through `merge_into`.

Every caller of the removed methods obtains merging, conversion, and assignment from these functions instead of keeping its own copy of the algorithms. That covers `BaseContainer.merge_with`, `OmegaConf.merge`, `OmegaConf.unsafe_merge`, the merge that assigns a structured config into a union-typed node, `OmegaConf.to_container`, and `OmegaConf.to_yaml`. It also covers every `DictConfig` and `ListConfig` route that stores an item: indexed assignment, attribute assignment, `append`, and `insert`. `BaseContainer` no longer defines `_merge_with`, `_map_merge`, `_list_merge`, `_tuple_merge`, `_to_content`, `_set_item_impl`, or `_wrap_value_and_set`. Type-hint propagation is shared the same way: merging and container assignment both obtain it from `apply_type_hint`, and no other copy of that algorithm remains in the package.

`omegaconf.container_ops` defines functions only. It introduces no class, and the method resolution order of `DictConfig`, `ListConfig`, and `TupleConfig` is unchanged. No class moves module, so a config pickled before this change still loads and compares equal afterwards. Importing `omegaconf.container_ops` in a fresh interpreter succeeds. The module never imports `omegaconf.basecontainer`, `omegaconf.dictconfig`, `omegaconf.listconfig`, `omegaconf.tupleconfig`, or `omegaconf.omegaconf`, at any scope. It never obtains their contents through the `omegaconf` package either. The dependency direction therefore runs from the containers to the operations.

Tests are run with `python3 -m pytest tests/` from the repository root.

records.description:
Move the knowledge of which JavaScript standard-library members TypeScriptToLua translates, and how, out of the hand-written `switch` statements in `src/transformation/builtins/` into a declarative registry, and make the builtin transformation read that registry. This is a behaviour-preserving restructuring: every program the type checker accepts transpiles to the same Lua, with the same diagnostics, as before.

Add `src/transformation/builtins/registry.ts` exporting a `builtinRegistry` object with four tables:

- `owners`: a record keyed by builtin owner. The owners are `Array`, `ArrayConstructor`, `String`, `StringConstructor`, `Number`, `NumberConstructor`, `Function`, `Math`, `ObjectConstructor`, `Console`, `MapConstructor`, `PromiseConstructor`, and `SymbolConstructor`.
- `globalCalls`: builtin identifiers that are called directly (`parseInt`, `isNaN`, `String(...)` and so on), keyed by the standard-library symbol name of the callee.
- `globalIdentifiers`: builtin identifiers used as values (`NaN`, `Infinity`, `globalThis`), keyed by identifier text.
- `typeFeatures`: standard-library type symbol names whose use imports a lualib feature (`Map`, `WeakSet`, `Promise`, the `Error` family and their constructors), each mapped to the `LuaLibFeature` it requires.

Each owner is a plain object with these fields:

- `kind`: `"prototype"` when its members are called on an instance, `"static"` when they are called on the owner itself.
- `diagnosticName`: the owner name that appears in the `unsupported property` diagnostic.
- `symbolNames`: the standard-library symbol names whose members belong to the owner.
- `prepareCall`: translates the receiver, when there is one, and the arguments of a call into `{ caller?, params }`.
- `methods` and `properties`: records of entries keyed by member name.

A method entry is one of three shapes. `{ kind: "lualib", feature }` means the member is translated to a call of that lualib feature with the receiver, when there is one, followed by the arguments. `{ kind: "custom", transform }` means `transform(context, node, calledMethod, call)` receives the prepared `{ caller?, params }` and returns the Lua expression. `{ kind: "unsupported" }` means the member is known and always reported. A property entry is `{ kind: "custom", transform }` with `transform(context, node)`, or `{ kind: "unsupported" }`. Every member that is translated today has an entry. Members the transformer reports as unsupported by name today are `unsupported` entries; for functions that is `toString` and the `name`, `arguments`, `caller`, and `displayName` properties, while `length` stays translated. Entries are looked up as own properties only, so a name inherited from `Object.prototype` is not an entry.

Also export from `registry.ts` the lookups `getBuiltinOwners()`, `getBuiltinOwnerForSymbol(symbolName, kind)`, `getBuiltinMethod(owner, name)`, `getBuiltinProperty(owner, name)`, `getBuiltinGlobalCall(symbolName)`, `getBuiltinGlobalIdentifier(identifierText)`, and `getLuaLibTypeFeature(symbolName)`. Each returns `undefined` when there is no entry. Export `getSupportedBuiltinMethods(owner)` and `getSupportedBuiltinProperties(owner)`, which list the member names whose entry is not `unsupported`.

The transformation in `src/transformation/builtins/index.ts` resolves the owner of an expression and then consults the registry at transformation time. Replacing or removing an entry in `builtinRegistry` before transpiling therefore changes the emitted Lua accordingly. For an owner whose unknown members are reported today, a call or property access with no entry is reported with the owner's `diagnosticName`. For `Function`, members without an entry fall through to the ordinary property and call transformation as they do today. An `Array` property access without an entry falls through the same way, while an `Array` method call without an entry is reported. The `Object.prototype` fallback for `toString` and `hasOwnProperty`, the optional-call diagnostic for static builtins, the lualib feature imports, and the order in which receivers and arguments are translated are unchanged.

Move the knowledge of which JavaScript standard-library members TypeScriptToLua translates, and how, out of the hand-written `switch` statements in `src/transformation/builtins/` into a declarative registry, and make the builtin transformation read that registry. This is a behaviour-preserving restructuring: every program the type checker accepts transpiles to the same Lua, with the same diagnostics, as before.

Add `src/transformation/builtins/registry.ts` exporting a `builtinRegistry` object with four tables:

- `owners`: a record keyed by builtin owner. The owners are `Array`, `ArrayConstructor`, `String`, `StringConstructor`, `Number`, `NumberConstructor`, `Function`, `Math`, `ObjectConstructor`, `Console`, `MapConstructor`, `PromiseConstructor`, and `SymbolConstructor`.
- `globalCalls`: builtin identifiers that are called directly (`parseInt`, `isNaN`, `String(...)` and so on), keyed by the standard-library symbol name of the callee.
- `globalIdentifiers`: builtin identifiers used as values (`NaN`, `Infinity`, `globalThis`), keyed by identifier text.
- `typeFeatures`: standard-library type symbol names whose use imports a lualib feature (`Map`, `WeakSet`, `Promise`, the `Error` family and their constructors), each mapped to the `LuaLibFeature` it requires.

Each owner is a plain object with these fields:

- `kind`: `"prototype"` when its members are called on an instance, `"static"` when they are called on the owner itself.
- `diagnosticName`: the owner name that appears in the `unsupported property` diagnostic.
- `symbolNames`: the standard-library symbol names whose members belong to the owner.
- `prepareCall`: translates the receiver, when there is one, and the arguments of a call into `{ caller?, params }`.
- `methods` and `properties`: records of entries keyed by member name.

A method entry is one of three shapes. `{ kind: "lualib", feature }` means the member is translated to a call of that lualib feature with the receiver, when there is one, followed by the arguments. `{ kind: "custom", transform }` means `transform(context, node, calledMethod, call)` receives the prepared `{ caller?, params }` and returns the Lua expression. `{ kind: "unsupported" }` means the member is known and always reported. A property entry is `{ kind: "custom", transform }` with `transform(context, node)`, or `{ kind: "unsupported" }`. Every member that is translated today has an entry. Members the transformer reports as unsupported by name today are `unsupported` entries; for functions that is `toString` and the `name`, `arguments`, `caller`, and `displayName` properties, while `length` stays translated. Entries are looked up as own properties only, so a name inherited from `Object.prototype` is not an entry.

Also export from `registry.ts` the lookups `getBuiltinOwners()`, `getBuiltinOwnerForSymbol(symbolName, kind)`, `getBuiltinMethod(owner, name)`, `getBuiltinProperty(owner, name)`, `getBuiltinGlobalCall(symbolName)`, `getBuiltinGlobalIdentifier(identifierText)`, and `getLuaLibTypeFeature(symbolName)`. Each returns `undefined` when there is no entry. Export `getSupportedBuiltinMethods(owner)` and `getSupportedBuiltinProperties(owner)`, which list the member names whose entry is not `unsupported`.

The transformation in `src/transformation/builtins/index.ts` resolves the owner of an expression and then consults the registry at transformation time. Replacing or removing an entry in `builtinRegistry` before transpiling therefore changes the emitted Lua accordingly. For an owner whose unknown members are reported today, a call or property access with no entry is reported with the owner's `diagnosticName`. For `Function`, members without an entry fall through to the ordinary property and call transformation as they do today. An `Array` property access without an entry falls through the same way, while an `Array` method call without an entry is reported. The `Object.prototype` fallback for `toString` and `hasOwnProperty`, the optional-call diagnostic for static builtins, the lualib feature imports, and the order in which receivers and arguments are translated are unchanged.

To get familiar with the current situation, here is a short overview of how the builtins are transformed and what should change. All the knowledge about which members of the JavaScript standard library we translate, and how, is in the switch statements in src/transformation/builtins, one file per owner. This works, but it is impractical to find out anything from it without reading every switch, and it makes it easy to make mistakes when adding a member.

Due to this we would like to have the same knowledge in a registry instead, and the builtin transformation should read from the registry. The registry is a new module src/transformation/builtins/registry.ts exporting a builtinRegistry object with four tables: owners, globalCalls, globalIdentifiers and typeFeatures. Owners are keyed by builtin owner. The owners are Array, ArrayConstructor, String, StringConstructor, Number, NumberConstructor, Function, Math, ObjectConstructor, Console, MapConstructor, PromiseConstructor and SymbolConstructor.

globalCalls is for the builtin identifiers that get called directly (parseInt, isNaN, String(...) and such). It is keyed by the standard library symbol name of the callee. globalIdentifiers is for the builtin identifiers used as a value (NaN, Infinity, globalThis) and is keyed by the identifier text. typeFeatures is for the standard library type symbol names which need a lualib feature when used, so Map, WeakSet, Promise, the Error family and their constructors. Each one is mapped to the LuaLibFeature it requires.

An owner is a plain object. It has a kind, which is "prototype" when its members are called on an instance and "static" when they are called on the owner itself. It has a diagnosticName, being the owner name that is shown in the unsupported property diagnostic. It has the symbolNames of the standard library whose members belong to it. It has a prepareCall function that translates the receiver (if there is one) and the arguments of a call into { caller?, params }. And it has the methods and properties records with the entries keyed by member name.

For a method entry there are three shapes. { kind: "lualib", feature } means the member is translated to a call of that lualib feature with the receiver, when there is one, followed by the arguments. { kind: "custom", transform } means transform(context, node, calledMethod, call) is given the prepared { caller?, params } and returns the Lua expression. { kind: "unsupported" } means the member is known and is always reported. A property entry is { kind: "custom", transform } with transform(context, node), or { kind: "unsupported" }. Every member that we translate today should get an entry. The members the transformer reports as unsupported by name today become unsupported entries. For functions that is toString and the name, arguments, caller and displayName properties. Entries are looked up as own properties only, so a name that is inherited from Object.prototype is not an entry.

From registry.ts we also want some lookups: getBuiltinOwners(), getBuiltinOwnerForSymbol(symbolName, kind), getBuiltinMethod(owner, name), getBuiltinProperty(owner, name), getBuiltinGlobalCall(symbolName), getBuiltinGlobalIdentifier(identifierText) and getLuaLibTypeFeature(symbolName). Each one returns undefined when there is no entry. Next to those, getSupportedBuiltinMethods(owner) and getSupportedBuiltinProperties(owner) list the member names whose entry is not unsupported.

The transformation in src/transformation/builtins/index.ts resolves the owner of an expression and then consults the registry at transformation time. So replacing or removing an entry in builtinRegistry before transpiling changes the emitted Lua accordingly. For an owner whose unknown members are reported today, a call or property access with no entry is reported with the diagnosticName of the owner. For Function, members without an entry fall through to the ordinary property and call transformation as they do today. An Array property access without an entry falls through the same way, while an Array method call without an entry is reported.

There is one file per owner (array.ts, string.ts, math.ts, and so on) and each has a switch over member names. That's where the actual knowledge is, which members we translate and what they turn into, but you can't find anything out without reading all of it. I'd rather this was a table.

What I have in mind is a registry module, src/transformation/builtins/registry.ts, which exports a builtinRegistry object. Four tables in there. owners is the main one, keyed by owner (Array, ArrayConstructor, String, StringConstructor, Number, NumberConstructor, Function, Math, ObjectConstructor, Console, MapConstructor, PromiseConstructor, SymbolConstructor, the same set we handle today). Then globalCalls for the builtins that are called as plain functions (parseInt, isNaN, String(...)), keyed by the callee's standard-library symbol name. globalIdentifiers for the ones used as a value, NaN and Infinity and globalThis, keyed by identifier text. typeFeatures for type symbol names that drag in a lualib feature when used (Map, WeakSet, Promise, the Error family, plus their constructors), mapped to the LuaLibFeature.

An owner record is a plain object. kind is "prototype" or "static" depending on whether members are called on an instance or on the owner. diagnosticName is what the unsupported property diagnostic prints. symbolNames is the list of standard-library symbols whose members belong to this owner. prepareCall turns the receiver (if any) and arguments of a call into { caller?, params }. methods and properties are records of entries, keyed by member name.

Three shapes of method entry. lualib with a feature: emit a call of that lualib feature, receiver first if there is one, then the arguments. custom with a transform: call transform(context, node, calledMethod, call) with the prepared { caller?, params } and use the Lua expression it returns. unsupported: known member, always reported. Property entries are custom (transform(context, node)) or unsupported. Everything translated today gets an entry; the members currently reported as unsupported by name (for Function that's toString, and the name/arguments/caller/displayName properties) become unsupported entries. Entries are looked up as own properties, so "constructor" or anything else off Object.prototype is not an entry.

Lookups, also exported from registry.ts: getBuiltinOwners(), getBuiltinOwnerForSymbol(symbolName, kind), getBuiltinMethod(owner, name), getBuiltinProperty(owner, name), getBuiltinGlobalCall(symbolName), getBuiltinGlobalIdentifier(identifierText), getLuaLibTypeFeature(symbolName). All return undefined for a miss. And getSupportedBuiltinMethods(owner) / getSupportedBuiltinProperties(owner), listing member names whose entry isn't unsupported.

index.ts then resolves the owner of an expression and looks the member up in the registry at transformation time (not at import time; if I delete an entry before transpiling, the Lua should change). Unknown members on owners that report today are still reported with the owner's diagnosticName. Function is the odd one out, members without an entry fall through to the ordinary property/call transformation, same as now. Array property access without an entry also falls through; an Array method call without an entry is reported.

None of this should change output. Any program the type checker accepts has to produce the same Lua and the same diagnostics as before. That includes the Object.prototype fallback for toString and hasOwnProperty, the optional-call diagnostic on static builtins, which lualib features get imported, and the order receivers and arguments are translated in.

records.description:
Here is a quick tour of the builtin transformation, so you know what lives where before you start changing things.

Running `npm run test:builtins` executes the whole builtin registry suite. That is the standard way to run everything.

Running everything takes a while, so during development of one part of the registry it is not practical to run every test each time. There are a few ways to make a test run faster:

If you open a pull request that adds functionality, we ask for registry tests to go with it, meaning tests that transpile and then execute the emitted Lua. They show that the new behaviour works now and keep showing it later.

We generally prefer not to have switch-based tests, because for most things the exact Lua text is not what matters; what matters is that running it gives the right answer, and that is what the registry tests check.

Coding style is mostly enforced by ESLint and Prettier. Run `npm run lint` to check your code before pushing. CI fails when the linter is unhappy. Installing the ESLint and Prettier extensions in your editor makes this a lot smoother.

A declarative registry of the builtins TypeScriptToLua translates. You declare an entry, and the transformation emits Lua.

When the builtin switches grow large it gets difficult to maintain and mistakes creep in easily. Writing the same knowledge as registry entries makes it more maintainable, more readable and more robust, and you get proper tooling on top, such as ESLint, Prettier, Visual Studio Code and WebStorm. It fits anywhere Lua is accepted, and existing members can simply be declared with TypeScript declaration files.

Install the `builtinRegistry` object to get started:

The package ships the `getBuiltinMethod` lookup, which works much like `getBuiltinProperty`:

The registry section in the documentation has more.

records.description:
The transpiler knows which parts of the JavaScript standard library it can turn into Lua, and what each one should become. Right now that knowledge is spread over a set of hand-written switch statements, one file per owner, under `src/transformation/builtins`. It works, but nothing can read it except a person going through every case by hand. Adding a member means finding the right arm in the right file, and forgetting one is easy.

This task gathers all of it into a single table that the transformation consults while it runs. The table is data. The code that translates a call or a property access looks the member up, finds out what to do, and does it. Nothing about the output changes. A program the type checker accepts comes out as the same Lua, with the same diagnostics, as it does today.

The table is a new module, `src/transformation/builtins/registry.ts`, which exports `builtinRegistry` with four parts: `owners`, `globalCalls`, `globalIdentifiers` and `typeFeatures`.

The owners are `Array`, `ArrayConstructor`, `String`, `StringConstructor`, `Number`, `NumberConstructor`, `Function`, `Math`, `ObjectConstructor`, `Console`, `MapConstructor`, `PromiseConstructor` and `SymbolConstructor`. Each is a plain object with `kind`, `diagnosticName`, `symbolNames`, `prepareCall`, `methods` and `properties`.

An owner is either the thing itself or its instances. That is what the kind says: static when members are called on the owner, prototype when they are called on an instance. The diagnostic name is the word the reader sees when a member is reported as unsupported. The symbol names are the standard-library symbols whose members belong to this owner. Preparing a call means translating the receiver, when there is one, and then the arguments; the result is the caller and the parameters, ready to be placed into whatever the entry decides to emit. Methods and properties are the two tables of entries, keyed by the member's name.

A method entry says one of three things. It can name a lualib feature, in which case the member becomes a call of that feature, receiver first if there is one, then the arguments. It can carry its own transform, which receives the prepared caller and parameters and returns the Lua expression. Or it can say the member is known but unsupported, so that it is always reported. A property entry is either a transform or unsupported. Written out, the shapes are `{ kind: "lualib", feature }`, `{ kind: "custom", transform }` with `transform(context, node, calledMethod, call)` for methods and `transform(context, node)` for properties, and `{ kind: "unsupported" }`.

Everything the transpiler translates today needs an entry. The members it reports as unsupported by name today become unsupported entries. For functions that is `toString`, and the properties `name`, `arguments`, `caller` and `displayName`. An entry is an own property of its table, so a name inherited from `Object.prototype` is not one.

Global calls are builtin functions called by name, like `parseInt`, `isNaN` or `String(...)`, keyed by the symbol name of the callee. Global identifiers are builtins used as a value, `NaN`, `Infinity` and `globalThis`, keyed by the identifier text. Type features are the standard-library types whose use brings in a lualib feature: `Map`, `WeakSet`, `Promise`, the `Error` family and their constructors, each mapped to its `LuaLibFeature`.

The module also exports the lookups `getBuiltinOwners()`, `getBuiltinOwnerForSymbol(symbolName, kind)`, `getBuiltinMethod(owner, name)`, `getBuiltinProperty(owner, name)`, `getBuiltinGlobalCall(symbolName)`, `getBuiltinGlobalIdentifier(identifierText)`, `getLuaLibTypeFeature(symbolName)`, `getSupportedBuiltinMethods(owner)` and `getSupportedBuiltinProperties(owner)`. A lookup that finds nothing returns undefined. The two listings give back the member names whose entry is not unsupported.

The transformation itself, in `src/transformation/builtins/index.ts`, first works out which owner an expression belongs to and then asks the table what to do, at the moment it is translating. So if an entry is replaced or removed before a program is transpiled, the Lua that comes out is different.

When a member has no entry, what happens depends on the owner. Owners that report unknown members today keep reporting them, using their diagnostic name. Functions are the exception: a function member with no entry is handled like any ordinary property or call, as it is now. Reading a property off an array with no entry is handled the same ordinary way, but calling an array method with no entry is reported.

Some things must stay exactly as they are. The fallback to `Object.prototype` for `toString` and `hasOwnProperty` stays. So does the diagnostic for an optional call on a static builtin, which lualib features get imported, and the order in which a receiver and its arguments are translated.

Move the knowledge of which JavaScript standard-library members TypeScriptToLua translates, and how, out of the hand-written `switch` statements in `src/transformation/builtins/` into a declarative registry, and make the builtin transformation read that registry. - `owners`: a record keyed by builtin owner. The owners are `Array`, `ArrayConstructor`, `String`, `StringConstructor`, `Number`, `NumberConstructor`, `Function`, `Math`, `ObjectConstructor`, `Console`, `MapConstructor`, `PromiseConstructor`, and `SymbolConstructor`.

- `globalIdentifiers`: builtin identifiers used as values (`NaN`, `Infinity`, `globalThis`), keyed by identifier text.
- `typeFeatures`: standard-library type symbol names whose use imports a lualib feature (`Map`, `WeakSet`, `Promise`, the `Error` family and their constructors), each mapped to the `LuaLibFeature` it requires.

Each owner is a plain object with these fields:

- `kind`: `"prototype"` when its members are called on an instance, `"static"` when they are called on the owner itself.
- `diagnosticName`: the owner name that appears in the `unsupported property` diagnostic.
- `symbolNames`: the standard-library symbol names whose members belong to the owner.
- `prepareCall`: translates the receiver, when there is one, and the arguments of a call into `{ caller?, params }`.
- `methods` and `properties`: records of entries keyed by member name.

A method entry is one of three shapes. `{ kind: "lualib", feature }` means the member is translated to a call of that lualib feature with the receiver, when there is one, followed by the arguments. `{ kind: "custom", transform }` means `transform(context, node, calledMethod, call)` receives the prepared `{ caller?, params }` and returns the Lua expression. `{ kind: "unsupported" }` means the member is known and always reported. Members the transformer reports as unsupported by name today are `unsupported` entries; for functions that is `toString` and the `name`, `arguments`, `caller`, and `displayName` properties, while `length` stays translated. Each returns `undefined` when there is no entry. Export `getSupportedBuiltinMethods(owner)` and `getSupportedBuiltinProperties(owner)`, which list the member names whose entry is not `unsupported`.

The transformation in `src/transformation/builtins/index.ts` resolves the owner of an expression and then consults the registry at transformation time. Replacing or removing an entry in `builtinRegistry` before transpiling therefore changes the emitted Lua accordingly. For an owner whose unknown members are reported today, a call or property access with no entry is reported with the owner's `diagnosticName`. For `Function`, members without an entry fall through to the ordinary property and call transformation as they do today. An `Array` property access without an entry falls through the same way, while an `Array` method call without an entry is reported. records.description:
Here is a quick tour of how builtins are transformed today, so you know where things live before you start changing them.

The code is under `src/transformation/builtins`. There is one file per owner: `array.ts`, `string.ts`, `number.ts`, `math.ts`, `function.ts`, `object.ts`, `console.ts`, `map.ts`, `promise.ts`, `symbol.ts` and `global.ts`. The entry points are in `index.ts`.

A property access goes through `transformBuiltinPropertyAccessExpression`. It asks the checker for the type of the expression on the left of the dot. When that expression is an identifier with a standard-library type, it switches on the symbol name: `NumberConstructor` goes to `transformNumberProperty`, `Math` to `transformMathProperty`, and `SymbolConstructor` just imports the `Symbol` lualib feature. Otherwise it checks whether the type is a string, an array or a function, and hands the node to the matching file.

A call goes through `transformBuiltinCallExpression`. If the callee is an identifier with a standard-library type, it first imports any lualib feature that type needs, then tries the global calls, such as `parseInt` or `Number(...)`. If the callee is a property access, it tries the static owners first, then the prototype owners, and last the `Object.prototype` fallback for `toString` and `hasOwnProperty`. That fallback runs even when the receiver has no resolved type, which is why `(foo as any).toString()` still works.

Inside each file the pattern is the same. Take `transformArrayConstructorCall` in `array.ts`. It resolves the signature, translates the arguments, and then switches on the member name. `from` and `isArray` become calls of the `ArrayFrom` and `ArrayIsArray` lualib functions. `of` becomes a table constructor around the arguments. Anything else pushes an `unsupported property` diagnostic that names the owner as `Array`.

The prototype files do the same with the receiver added. In `string.ts`, `transformStringPrototypeCall` translates the receiver and the arguments together, then switches on the name. `replace` and `split` go to lualib, while `charAt` and `slice` are written out inline. The default arm reports the member as `string.<name>`. `function.ts` is a little different: it emits the self-conversion diagnostic before it looks at the member, and its default arm does not report anything, so an unknown function member falls through to the ordinary call transformation.

Not every owner reports unknown members. `Function` does not, as above. Array property access does not either, because `transformArrayProperty` handles `length` and returns undefined for anything else. Every other owner has a `default:` arm that pushes the diagnostic.

Diagnostics use the base name of the owner, not the symbol name. That is why the message says `string.localeCompare is unsupported.` rather than mentioning `String`, and `Array.nothingLikeThis is unsupported.` for a static call.

The lualib imports for types are separate from the calls. `checkForLuaLibType` looks at a type's symbol name and imports `Map`, `Set`, `WeakMap`, `WeakSet`, `Promise` or `Error` when a program uses one of those, including their constructor types. The `Error` case covers `RangeError`, `ReferenceError`, `SyntaxError`, `TypeError` and `URIError` too.

All of this is covered by the existing tests. The builtin tests under `test/unit/builtins` transpile small programs and run the Lua, and the diagnostic messages are pinned by name.

records.description:
The builtin code under `src/transformation/builtins` is not hard to follow, but it is tedious to work in. Every owner has its own file, every file has a big switch over member names, and the only way to find out what we translate is to read all of them. Adding a member is easy enough once you have found the right arm; finding it is the slow part. It is also easy to get a diagnostic name wrong, because each file spells its own.

I would much rather have this as a table, and I think it is worth the churn. So this task moves the knowledge into a registry, and the transformation reads from it while it runs. Nothing about the output should move. A program the type checker accepts has to come out as the same Lua, with the same diagnostics, as it does today.

The registry is a new module, `src/transformation/builtins/registry.ts`, exporting `builtinRegistry`. It has four parts: `owners`, `globalCalls`, `globalIdentifiers` and `typeFeatures`. The owners are the thirteen we handle now, `Array`, `ArrayConstructor`, `String`, `StringConstructor`, `Number`, `NumberConstructor`, `Function`, `Math`, `ObjectConstructor`, `Console`, `MapConstructor`, `PromiseConstructor` and `SymbolConstructor`.

An owner is a plain object, nothing clever. `kind` is `"static"` when members are called on the owner and `"prototype"` when they are called on an instance; that distinction already exists, it is just implicit today. `diagnosticName` is the word the diagnostic prints, which matters more than it looks because people grep for it. `symbolNames` are the standard-library symbols whose members belong here. `prepareCall` translates the receiver, when there is one, and then the arguments into `{ caller?, params }`; this is the bit each owner does slightly differently now, so it stays per owner. `methods` and `properties` are the two tables of entries, keyed by member name.

A method entry is one of three things, and honestly three is plenty. `{ kind: "lualib", feature }` is the common case: the member becomes a call of that lualib feature, receiver first if there is one, then the arguments. `{ kind: "custom", transform }` is for the awkward ones; `transform(context, node, calledMethod, call)` gets the prepared `{ caller?, params }` and returns the Lua expression. `{ kind: "unsupported" }` is for members we know about and refuse, so they are always reported. Property entries are simpler: `{ kind: "custom", transform }` with `transform(context, node)`, or `{ kind: "unsupported" }`.

Everything we translate today needs an entry, which is most of the work. The members we report as unsupported by name today become unsupported entries; for functions that is `toString` and the `name`, `arguments`, `caller` and `displayName` properties. Entries must be own properties, because otherwise `"constructor"` would look like a member and that is a nasty surprise.

Global calls are the builtins called as plain functions, `parseInt`, `isNaN`, `String(...)` and friends. They are keyed by the callee's symbol name. Global identifiers are the ones used as a value, `NaN`, `Infinity`, `globalThis`, keyed by the identifier text. Type features are the standard-library types whose mere use pulls in a lualib feature, `Map`, `WeakSet`, `Promise`, the `Error` family and their constructors, each mapped to its `LuaLibFeature`.

The lookups are the boring part. `registry.ts` exports `getBuiltinOwners()`, `getBuiltinOwnerForSymbol(symbolName, kind)`, `getBuiltinMethod(owner, name)`, `getBuiltinProperty(owner, name)`, `getBuiltinGlobalCall(symbolName)`, `getBuiltinGlobalIdentifier(identifierText)` and `getLuaLibTypeFeature(symbolName)`. All of them return undefined on a miss. There are also `getSupportedBuiltinMethods(owner)` and `getSupportedBuiltinProperties(owner)` for the member names whose entry is not unsupported.

The part that actually matters is that `src/transformation/builtins/index.ts` asks the registry at transformation time, not once at import. The test I care about is simple: replace or remove an entry in `builtinRegistry` before transpiling and the Lua changes. If it does not, the registry is decoration.

Unknown members keep their current fate, which is a little uneven and I am fine with that. Owners that report unknown members today still do, with their diagnostic name. Functions are the exception and always were; a function member with no entry falls through to the ordinary property and call handling. Reading a property off an array with no entry falls through the same way, but calling an array method with no entry is reported.

A few things must not move at all. The `Object.prototype` fallback for `toString` and `hasOwnProperty` stays. So does the diagnostic for an optional call on a static builtin, which lualib features get imported, and the order a receiver and its arguments are translated in. They are the sort of thing that breaks quietly.

records.description:
TypeScriptToLua supports builtins - an interface that allows to customize how standard library members are translated. Internally, to process a call or property access on a standard library type, TypeScriptToLua resolves the owner of the member and looks the member up. Today, `src/transformation/builtins/` has the switch statements for the builtins in its files, one file per owner. This task replaces them with a registry: to add a builtin you have to add it under the `builtinRegistry` object in `src/transformation/builtins/registry.ts`, and the transformation reads that object instead of the switch statements. The registry keeps identical behavior for every program the type checker accepts: the same Lua, with the same diagnostics, as before.

The registry allows passing owner records and providing different kinds of entries, such as the lualib feature to be used to translate a member. The tables in this object are:

- `owners: Record<string, BuiltinOwner>` - A record of owner name keys and owner values. The owners are `Array`, `ArrayConstructor`, `String`, `StringConstructor`, `Number`, `NumberConstructor`, `Function`, `Math`, `ObjectConstructor`, `Console`, `MapConstructor`, `PromiseConstructor` and `SymbolConstructor`.
- `globalCalls: Record<string, BuiltinEntry>` - A record of callee symbol name keys (`parseInt`, `isNaN`, and `StringConstructor` for `String(...)`) and entry values.
- `globalIdentifiers: Record<string, BuiltinEntry>` - A record of identifier text keys (`NaN`, `Infinity`, `globalThis`) and entry values.
- `typeFeatures: Record<string, LuaLibFeature>` - A record of type symbol name keys (`Map`, `WeakSet`, `Promise`, the `Error` family and their constructors) and `LuaLibFeature` values, the feature that using the type imports.

An owner is a plain object (like an object literal for example) where keys are the fields below, and values describe how the members of that owner are translated. The fields in this object are:

- `kind: "prototype" | "static"` - This specifies whether members are called on an instance (`"prototype"`) or on the owner itself (`"static"`).
- `diagnosticName: string` - The owner name to report in the `unsupported property` diagnostic.
- `symbolNames: string[]` - An array of standard-library symbol names to be resolved to the owner.
- `prepareCall` - Provides a callback to use to translate the receiver, when there is one, and the arguments of a call into `{ caller?, params }`.
- `methods`, `properties: Record<string, BuiltinEntry>` - A record of member name keys and entry values.

Make sure that every member the transpiler translates today has an entry, and set the value of `kind` on each. Valid values are `"lualib"`, `"custom"` and `"unsupported"`. TypeScriptToLua relies on the lualib for `{ kind: "lualib", feature }` entries. In other words, it transpiles the member to a call of that lualib feature, with the receiver (when there is one) followed by the arguments. A custom transform, `{ kind: "custom", transform }`, is a function, called with a prepared call and transformation context, and returning a Lua AST node: `transform(context, node, calledMethod, call)`, where `call` is the prepared `{ caller?, params }`. (For a property transform there is no `call`.)

`{ kind: "unsupported" }` entries are not translated at all. Instead, the member is reported, the same as today. Note that we assume that the registry is complete in this sense, and that members it reports by name today have an `unsupported` entry: for functions that is `toString` and the `name`/`arguments`/`caller`/`displayName` properties. `length` is not affected and stays translated. When looking up an entry, this only affects the owner's own entries. It will not find names inherited from `Object.prototype`, such as `constructor`.

Tests can inject their own entries using the `builtinRegistry` object, or remove entries, before transpiling, overriding standard transformation behavior: the transformation reads the registry at transformation time, and the emitted Lua changes accordingly. Members that are handled outside the registry will not be affected: the `Object.prototype` fallback for `toString` and `hasOwnProperty`; the optional-call diagnostic for static builtins; the lualib feature imports; and the order in which receivers and arguments are translated.

`registry.ts` also exports the lookups `getBuiltinOwners()`, `getBuiltinOwnerForSymbol(symbolName, kind)`, `getBuiltinMethod(owner, name)`, `getBuiltinProperty(owner, name)`, `getBuiltinGlobalCall(symbolName)`, `getBuiltinGlobalIdentifier(identifierText)` and `getLuaLibTypeFeature(symbolName)`. records.summary: The description is detailed but largely load-bearing for the registry API and behavior that the hidden tests exercise; only its API-list scaffolding could be made more compact.
records.description:
TypeScriptToLua supports builtins - an interface that allows to customize how standard library members are translated. Internally, to process a call or property access on a standard library type, TypeScriptToLua resolves the owner of the member and looks the member up. Today, `src/transformation/builtins/` has the switch statements for the builtins in its files, one file per owner. This task replaces them with a registry: to add a builtin you have to add it under the `builtinRegistry` object in `src/transformation/builtins/registry.ts`, and the transformation reads that object instead of the switch statements. The registry keeps identical behavior for every program the type checker accepts: the same Lua, with the same diagnostics, as before.

The registry allows passing owner records and providing different kinds of entries, such as the lualib feature to be used to translate a member. The tables in this object are:

- `owners: Record<string, BuiltinOwner>` - A record of owner name keys and owner values. The owners are `Array`, `ArrayConstructor`, `String`, `StringConstructor`, `Number`, `NumberConstructor`, `Function`, `Math`, `ObjectConstructor`, `Console`, `MapConstructor`, `PromiseConstructor` and `SymbolConstructor`.
- `globalCalls: Record<string, BuiltinEntry>` - A record of callee symbol name keys (`parseInt`, `isNaN`, and `StringConstructor` for `String(...)`) and entry values.
- `globalIdentifiers: Record<string, BuiltinEntry>` - A record of identifier text keys (`NaN`, `Infinity`, `globalThis`) and entry values.
- `typeFeatures: Record<string, LuaLibFeature>` - A record of type symbol name keys (`Map`, `WeakSet`, `Promise`, the `Error` family and their constructors) and `LuaLibFeature` values, the feature that using the type imports.

An owner is a plain object (like an object literal for example) where keys are the fields below, and values describe how the members of that owner are translated. The fields in this object are:

- `kind: "prototype" | "static"` - This specifies whether members are called on an instance (`"prototype"`) or on the owner itself (`"static"`).
- `diagnosticName: string` - The owner name to report in the `unsupported property` diagnostic.
- `symbolNames: string[]` - An array of standard-library symbol names to be resolved to the owner.
- `prepareCall` - Provides a callback to use to translate the receiver, when there is one, and the arguments of a call into `{ caller?, params }`.
- `methods`, `properties: Record<string, BuiltinEntry>` - A record of member name keys and entry values.

Make sure that every member the transpiler translates today has an entry, and set the value of `kind` on each. Valid values are `"lualib"`, `"custom"` and `"unsupported"`. TypeScriptToLua relies on the lualib for `{ kind: "lualib", feature }` entries. In other words, it transpiles the member to a call of that lualib feature, with the receiver (when there is one) followed by the arguments. A custom transform, `{ kind: "custom", transform }`, is a function, called with a prepared call and transformation context, and returning a Lua AST node: `transform(context, node, calledMethod, call)`, where `call` is the prepared `{ caller?, params }`. (For a property transform there is no `call`.)

`{ kind: "unsupported" }` entries are not translated at all. Instead, the member is reported, the same as today. Note that we assume that the registry is complete in this sense, and that members it reports by name today have an `unsupported` entry: for functions that is `toString` and the `name`/`arguments`/`caller`/`displayName` properties. `length` is not affected and stays translated. When looking up an entry, this only affects the owner's own entries. It will not find names inherited from `Object.prototype`, such as `constructor`.

Tests can inject their own entries using the `builtinRegistry` object, or remove entries, before transpiling, overriding standard transformation behavior: the transformation reads the registry at transformation time, and the emitted Lua changes accordingly. Behavior that the registry does not decide will not be affected: the `Object.prototype` fallback for `toString` and `hasOwnProperty`; the optional-call diagnostic for static builtins; how a lualib feature is imported once an entry names it; and the order in which receivers and arguments are translated.

`registry.ts` also exports the lookups `getBuiltinOwners()`, `getBuiltinOwnerForSymbol(symbolName, kind)`, `getBuiltinMethod(owner, name)`, `getBuiltinProperty(owner, name)`, `getBuiltinGlobalCall(symbolName)`, `getBuiltinGlobalIdentifier(identifierText)` and `getLuaLibTypeFeature(symbolName)`. If a lookup finds no entry, it returns `undefined`. `getSupportedBuiltinMethods(owner)` and `getSupportedBuiltinProperties(owner)` return the member names whose entry is not `unsupported`.

There is a subtle difference between owners for members without an entry. For an owner that reports unknown members today, a member without an entry is reported with the owner's `diagnosticName`, the same as an unknown member. `Function` members without an entry: Not reported. Use the ordinary property and call transformation instead, as tstl does today. `Array` property accesses without an entry work the same way, but an `Array` method call without an entry is reported.

records.summary: The task is detailed but mostly load-bearing for the extraction and parity tests; only a small amount of introductory and submission-specific detail can be trimmed.
records.description:
OmegaConf containers look similar to Python dictionaries, lists, and tuples, but are not native containers. Use `to_content(conf, resolve, throw_on_missing, enum_to_str=False, structured_config_mode=SCMode.DICT, resolved_node_cache=None, encode_missing_literals=False)` to convert them to plain dictionaries, lists, and tuples. If `resolve` is set to `True`, interpolations will be resolved during conversion. You can control how missing values are handled by `to_content()` using the `throw_on_missing` keyword argument. Setting `throw_on_missing=True` can be useful if you want your program to fail fast when there are missing values in the config. You can customize the treatment of `to_content()` for Structured Config nodes using the `structured_config_mode` option. Using `structured_config_mode=SCMode.INSTANTIATE`, Structured Config nodes are converted to instances of the backing dataclass or attrs class.

OmegaConf offers a second place to reach this conversion: `container_ops`. The upside is that the dependency runs one way: `container_ops` never imports `omegaconf.basecontainer`, `omegaconf.dictconfig`, `omegaconf.listconfig`, `omegaconf.tupleconfig` or `omegaconf.omegaconf` back, at any scope, nor through the `omegaconf` package.

OmegaConf supports merging configs together, as well as assigning into them. This means some type hints can not be applied by the containers alone, and `apply_type_hint(node, type_hint)` is required. A value of the declared type can be assigned directly. The call `set_item(target, key, value)` is equivalent to `BaseContainer._set_item_impl(target, key, value)` today, and `apply_type_hint(node, type_hint)` is equivalent to `_deep_update_type_hint(node, type_hint)` in `omegaconf.basecontainer`.

In 2.4, direct assignment and typed list or dict mutations of convertible values still convert, but emit a `FutureWarning`. Supply values of the declared type to avoid the warning. Assigning a list to a tuple-typed field, or a tuple to a list-typed field, also warns. Runtime validation and conversion works for all supported types, including Enums. OmegaConf will validate that assignment of nested objects is of the correct type. OmegaConf verifies at runtime that your Lists contains only values of the correct type.

OmegaConf offers a second faster function to merge config objects: `merge_into(target, *sources, allow_readonly_target=False)`. Unlike `OmegaConf.merge()`, `merge_into()` is merging into the target in place and the sources should no longer be used after this call. A plain dict can appear on the source side. OmegaConf support several configuration flags. Configuration flags can be set on any configuration node (Sequence or Mapping). If a configuration flag is not set it inherits the value from the parent of the node, and `merge_into` honours `allow_objects` the same way. A read-only configuration cannot be modified. An attempt to modify it will result in omegaconf.ReadonlyConfigError exception. You can temporarily remove the read only flag from a config object with `allow_readonly_target=True`.

Merging configurations enables the creation of reusable configuration files for each logical component instead of a single config file for each variation of your task. OmegaConf offers a second faster function to merge config objects: `OmegaConf.unsafe_merge()`. Unlike `OmegaConf.merge()`, `unsafe_merge()` is destroying the input configs and they should no longer be used after this call. The upside is that it's substantially faster. Once `merge_into` is in place, every merge goes through it regardless of its entry point: `OmegaConf.merge()`, `OmegaConf.unsafe_merge()`, `BaseContainer.merge_with()` and the assignment of a structured config into a union-typed node. The target's kind controls which merge is used: `map_merge(dest, src, allow_readonly_target=False)` for a `DictConfig`, `list_merge(dest, src)` for a `ListConfig`, and `tuple_merge(dest, src)` for a `TupleConfig` receiving a `ListConfig` or a `TupleConfig`.

By default, OmegaConf dictionaries allow write access to unknown fields. Indexed assignment, attribute assignment, `append` and `insert` on `DictConfig` and `ListConfig` all write through `set_item(target, key, value)`. Interpolated values are validated, and converted when possible, to the annotated type when the interpolation is accessed; the type hint itself is propagated by `apply_type_hint(node, type_hint)`, from merging and from assignment, and nowhere else.

Use pickle to save and load while retaining the type information. Note that the saved file may be incompatible across different versions of OmegaConf, but a config pickled before this change still loads and compares equal afterwards: `DictConfig`, `ListConfig` and `TupleConfig` keep their module and method resolution order. `BaseContainer` no longer defines `_merge_with`, `_map_merge`, `_list_merge`, `_tuple_merge`, `_to_content`, `_set_item_impl` and `_wrap_value_and_set`. `omegaconf.container_ops` defines functions only. Values, node types and metadata, flags, parent links, warnings and errors are not affected.

When submitting a PR please ensure that it includes a one-line news fragment under the `news` folder (valid extensions are: `.feature`, `.bugfix`, `.api_change`, `.docs`, `.misc`), here `news/1349.misc`. Run tests directly with `pytest`: `python3 -m pytest tests/` from the repository root.

records.summary: The description is concise prose and its detailed behavioral requirements closely track the tested generator-completion cases; only one implementation-oriented aside can be trimmed.
records.description:
Generators in Lua work quite differently than in TypeScript/JavaScript, so a special runtime is needed to use them. Because Lua doesn't have a strictly defined concept of a generator, for TypeScriptToLua a `function*` declaration implies a very specific structure, built specifically for TypeScript compatibility. Because of that, the object it returns has a `next` method and no `return` or `throw` that a caller can use. Below are some of the cases where the resulting generator has to behave the same as compiled JS.

All generator objects, by default, have a `return(value)` method and a `throw(error)` method to preserve JavaScript behaviour. The injected completion occurs at the suspended `yield`. A thrown completion runs `catch` and `finally` blocks, while a return completion runs only `finally` blocks. Generators that yield again inside `finally` will not be affected and stay suspended there. The `return` written inside `finally` is called _after_ the requested completion has been injected, so it takes precedence over that completion.

Calling `return` before the first `next` is the same as if the generator had finished, so the body is not entered. After completion, `return(value)` must produce `{ value, done: true }`, while `throw(error)` must rethrow the supplied error. Some generators are closed before a `for...of`, spread or destructuring reaches them (for example, if `return` was called on them earlier). These can be iterated without resuming the body, and produce nothing. Some generators can be reached with `next`, `return` or `throw` while they are still running (for example, from a callback the body itself called). This throws a `TypeError` because a running generator is not assignable to a suspended one.

Lua coroutines support passing an invisible value each resume. If your delegate does this, the argument of the outer `next` is passed on to the delegate's `next`. The `return` and `throw` methods are called on the delegate of a `yield*` _when it has them_, before resolving the completion in the outer generator. If the delegate reports `done: true`, a forwarded `return` finishes the outer generator with that value, and a forwarded `throw` is the value of the `yield*` expression. If the delegate reports `done: false`, the outer generator yields that result and delegation continues. Some delegates do not have a `return` method (for example, arrays and strings). In this case, a forwarded `return` finishes the outer generator with the requested value. Some delegates do not have a `throw` method. This throws a `TypeError` after the delegate's `return` has been called when present.

These semantics apply to the default Lua target. Closing an iterator when a `for-of` loop exits early is outside scope.

records.description:
OmegaConf containers look similar to Python dictionaries, lists, and tuples, but are not native containers. Use `to_content(conf, resolve, throw_on_missing, enum_to_str=False, structured_config_mode=SCMode.DICT, resolved_node_cache=None, encode_missing_literals=False)` to convert them to plain dictionaries, lists, and tuples. If `resolve` is set to `True`, interpolations will be resolved during conversion. You can control how missing values are handled by `to_content()` using the `throw_on_missing` keyword argument. Setting `throw_on_missing=True` can be useful if you want your program to fail fast when there are missing values in the config. You can customize the treatment of `to_content()` for Structured Config nodes using the `structured_config_mode` option. Using `structured_config_mode=SCMode.INSTANTIATE`, Structured Config nodes are converted to instances of the backing dataclass or attrs class.

OmegaConf offers a second place to reach this conversion: `container_ops`. The upside is that the dependency runs one way: `container_ops` never imports `omegaconf.basecontainer`, `omegaconf.dictconfig`, `omegaconf.listconfig`, `omegaconf.tupleconfig` or `omegaconf.omegaconf` back, at any scope, nor through the `omegaconf` package.

OmegaConf supports merging configs together, as well as assigning into them. This means some type hints can not be applied by the containers alone, and `apply_type_hint(node, type_hint)` is required. A value of the declared type can be assigned directly. The call `set_item(target, key, value)` is equivalent to `BaseContainer._set_item_impl(target, key, value)` today, and `apply_type_hint(node, type_hint)` is equivalent to `_deep_update_type_hint(node, type_hint)` in `omegaconf.basecontainer`.

In 2.4, direct assignment and typed list or dict mutations of convertible values still convert, but emit a `FutureWarning`. Supply values of the declared type to avoid the warning. Assigning a list to a tuple-typed field, or a tuple to a list-typed field, also warns. Runtime validation and conversion works for all supported types, including Enums. OmegaConf will validate that assignment of nested objects is of the correct type. OmegaConf verifies at runtime that your Lists contains only values of the correct type.

OmegaConf offers a second faster function to merge config objects: `merge_into(target, *sources, allow_readonly_target=False)`. Unlike `OmegaConf.merge()`, `merge_into()` is merging into the target in place and the sources should no longer be used after this call. A plain dict can appear on the source side. OmegaConf support several configuration flags. Configuration flags can be set on any configuration node (Sequence or Mapping). If a configuration flag is not set it inherits the value from the parent of the node, and `merge_into` honours `allow_objects` the same way. A read-only configuration cannot be modified. An attempt to modify it will result in omegaconf.ReadonlyConfigError exception. You can temporarily remove the read only flag from a config object with `allow_readonly_target=True`.

Merging configurations enables the creation of reusable configuration files for each logical component instead of a single config file for each variation of your task. OmegaConf offers a second faster function to merge config objects: `OmegaConf.unsafe_merge()`. Unlike `OmegaConf.merge()`, `unsafe_merge()` is destroying the input configs and they should no longer be used after this call. The upside is that it's substantially faster. Once `merge_into` is in place, every merge goes through it regardless of its entry point: `OmegaConf.merge()`, `OmegaConf.unsafe_merge()`, `BaseContainer.merge_with()` and the assignment of a structured config into a union-typed node. The target's kind controls which merge is used: `map_merge(dest, src, allow_readonly_target=False)` for a `DictConfig`, `list_merge(dest, src)` for a `ListConfig`, and `tuple_merge(dest, src)` for a `TupleConfig` receiving a `ListConfig` or a `TupleConfig`.

By default, OmegaConf dictionaries allow write access to unknown fields. Indexed assignment, attribute assignment, `append` and `insert` on `DictConfig` and `ListConfig` all write through `set_item(target, key, value)`. Interpolated values are validated, and converted when possible, to the annotated type when the interpolation is accessed; the type hint itself is propagated by `apply_type_hint(node, type_hint)`, from merging and from assignment, and nowhere else.

Use pickle to save and load while retaining the type information. Note that the saved file may be incompatible across different versions of OmegaConf, but a config pickled before this change still loads and compares equal afterwards: `DictConfig`, `ListConfig` and `TupleConfig` keep their module and method resolution order. `BaseContainer` no longer defines `_merge_with`, `_map_merge`, `_list_merge`, `_tuple_merge`, `_to_content`, `_set_item_impl` and `_wrap_value_and_set`. `omegaconf.container_ops` defines functions only. Values, node types and metadata, flags, parent links, warnings and errors are not affected.

records.description:
TypeScriptToLua supports builtins - an interface that allows to customize how standard library members are translated. Internally, to process a call or property access on a standard library type, TypeScriptToLua resolves the owner of the member and looks the member up. Today, `src/transformation/builtins/` has the switch statements for the builtins in its files, one file per owner. This task replaces them with a registry: to add a builtin you have to add it under the `builtinRegistry` object in `src/transformation/builtins/registry.ts`, and the transformation reads that object instead of the switch statements. The registry keeps identical behavior for every program the type checker accepts: the same Lua, with the same diagnostics, as before.

The registry allows passing owner records and providing different kinds of entries, such as the lualib feature to be used to translate a member. The tables in this object are:

- `owners: Record<string, BuiltinOwner>` - A record of owner name keys and owner values. The owners are `Array`, `ArrayConstructor`, `String`, `StringConstructor`, `Number`, `NumberConstructor`, `Function`, `Math`, `ObjectConstructor`, `Console`, `MapConstructor`, `PromiseConstructor` and `SymbolConstructor`.
- `globalCalls: Record<string, BuiltinEntry>` - A record of callee symbol name keys (`parseInt`, `isNaN`, and `StringConstructor` for `String(...)`) and entry values.
- `globalIdentifiers: Record<string, BuiltinEntry>` - A record of identifier text keys (`NaN`, `Infinity`, `globalThis`) and entry values.
- `typeFeatures: Record<string, LuaLibFeature>` - A record of type symbol name keys (`Map`, `WeakSet`, `Promise`, the `Error` family and their constructors) and `LuaLibFeature` values, the feature that using the type imports.

An owner is a plain object (like an object literal for example) where keys are the fields below, and values describe how the members of that owner are translated. The fields in this object are:

- `kind: "prototype" | "static"` - This specifies whether members are called on an instance (`"prototype"`) or on the owner itself (`"static"`).
- `diagnosticName: string` - The owner name to report in the `unsupported property` diagnostic.
- `symbolNames: string[]` - An array of standard-library symbol names to be resolved to the owner.
- `prepareCall` - Provides a callback to use to translate the receiver, when there is one, and the arguments of a call into `{ caller?, params }`.
- `methods`, `properties: Record<string, BuiltinEntry>` - A record of member name keys and entry values.

Make sure that every member the transpiler translates today has an entry, and set the value of `kind` on each. Valid values are `"lualib"`, `"custom"` and `"unsupported"`. TypeScriptToLua relies on the lualib for `{ kind: "lualib", feature }` entries. In other words, it transpiles the member to a call of that lualib feature, with the receiver (when there is one) followed by the arguments. A custom transform, `{ kind: "custom", transform }`, is a function, called with a prepared call and transformation context, and returning a Lua AST node: `transform(context, node, calledMethod, call)`, where `call` is the prepared `{ caller?, params }`. (For a property transform there is no `call`.)

`{ kind: "unsupported" }` entries are not translated at all. Instead, the member is reported, the same as today. Note that we assume that the registry is complete in this sense, and that members it reports by name today have an `unsupported` entry: for functions that is `toString` and the `name`/`arguments`/`caller`/`displayName` properties. `length` is not affected and stays translated. When looking up an entry, this only affects the owner's own entries. It will not find names inherited from `Object.prototype`, such as `constructor`.

Tests can inject their own entries using the `builtinRegistry` object, or remove entries, before transpiling, overriding standard transformation behavior: the transformation reads the registry at transformation time, and the emitted Lua changes accordingly. Behavior that the registry does not decide will not be affected: the `Object.prototype` fallback for `toString` and `hasOwnProperty`; the optional-call diagnostic for static builtins; how a lualib feature is imported once an entry names it; and the order in which receivers and arguments are translated.

`registry.ts` also exports the lookups `getBuiltinOwners()`, `getBuiltinOwnerForSymbol(symbolName, kind)`, `getBuiltinMethod(ownerName, name)`, `getBuiltinProperty(ownerName, name)`, `getBuiltinGlobalCall(symbolName)`, `getBuiltinGlobalIdentifier(identifierText)` and `getLuaLibTypeFeature(symbolName)`. If a lookup finds no entry, it returns `undefined`. `getSupportedBuiltinMethods(ownerName)` and `getSupportedBuiltinProperties(ownerName)` return the member names whose entry is not `unsupported`.

There is a subtle difference between owners for members without an entry. For an owner that reports unknown members today, a member without an entry is reported with the owner's `diagnosticName`, the same as an unknown member. `Function` members without an entry: Not reported. Use the ordinary property and call transformation instead, as tstl does today. `Array` property accesses without an entry work the same way, but an `Array` method call without an entry is reported.
